Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Denver/Boulder CO
538 AM MDT Sun Aug 30 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Active monsoon pattern continues Sunday and Monday.

- Warm and dry pattern returns for most of the upcoming week.

&&

.DISCUSSION /Through Saturday/...
Issued at 1222 AM MDT Sun Aug 30 2026

There haven't been too many significant changes in the large scale
pattern over the last 24 hours. A broad upper ridge remains
centered over the south central CONUS, with a trough noted over
the northern Rockies... leaving the area in broad southwesterly
flow aloft. This also puts us square in the middle of the
monsoonal moisture, and there's been a good amount of
precipitation falling across northwestern Colorado, which has
spread as far east as Grand/Jackson county.

Overnight CAMs are actually in decent agreement in how today's
convective potential plays out. Most guidance pushes a cluster of
showers and thunderstorms across Middle/North Park late this
morning into the early afternoon, which then advances east into
the Front Range and I-25 corridor by early/mid afternoon. The
convective environment is marginally favorable across most of the
lower elevations, with modest MLCAPE (~500 J/kg) but increased
deep layer shear. We can't totally rule out a few strong to severe
wind gusts with any stronger showers/storms as convection
continues to push eastward through the afternoon and evening
hours.

Monday still looks to feature the best chance of precipitation
across most of our forecast area, as a more pronounced shortwave
races across the state during the afternoon/early overnight hours.
There's timing differences across the various models, but
reasonably good agreement that a convective cluster will develop
across southwestern Colorado during the day, advancing into our
forecast area by the mid/late afternoon hours. Like the past few
days, meager surface/boundary layer moisture will limit
instability, but the stronger synoptic forcing should lead to more
widespread rainfall into Monday evening/Monday night. 

By Tuesday, the center of the 500mb ridge should slide east into 
the Ohio Valley, while a strong closed low spins off the coast of 
British Columbia. Across the region, southwesterly flow aloft will
persist. Moisture will diminish through this timeframe, with 
enough drying by Wednesday and Thursday that only a couple of 
weak showers are in the forecast across the the high country. 

The forecast pattern becomes a bit more complex as we approach
next weekend. The closed low near the Pacific Northwest coastline 
will eventually drift onshore, and its approach towards our area
should lead to a more poleward component of the mid/upper level
winds. Further complicating the pattern is the potential tropical
cyclone development across the eastern Pacific, which could
contribute to additional tropical moisture advection into the
region by next weekend. There is a fairly large spread across the
overnight guidance and it'll likely be a while until we have a
better handle on things, but the overall pattern would suggest
that we'll see precipitation chances increase towards the end of
our forecast period.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z TAFS through 12Z Monday/...
Issued at 528 AM MDT Sun Aug 30 2026

VFR conditions are expected through the TAF period. Main concern
through tonight is the potential for one or two clusters of
convection to bring variable/gusty outflow winds this afternoon
into the early evening hours.

Light drainage flow should turn clockwise through the morning
hours with speeds remaining generally light. Most guidance brings
a cluster of SHRA/TSRA through the terminals between about 20-02z.
There's a little more moisture/instability compared to the last
couple days and, but outflow winds are more likely than direct TS
impacts. A few showers may linger beyond 00z with winds quickly
turning to the southeast, with drainage likely establishing by
around 06z.  

&&

.BOU WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z TAFS through 18Z Monday/...
Issued at 1145 AM MDT Sun Aug 30 2026

Radar as of 1745z shows a broken line of showers and 
thunderstorms moving through Grand, Jackson, and western Larimer 
counties. Based on the latest radar trends and CAMs, have kept a 
TEMPO and VCSH starting at 20z (adjusted KBJC to start at 19z) 
for the possibility of high-based showers and thunderstorms for 
much of the afternoon. These could bring gusty outflow winds in 
excess of 35 kts, rain, and briefly lowering ceilings. There is a 
~30-40% chance that showers and thunderstorms linger through about
4z this evening. Behind the convection, winds should turn to 
drainage rather quickly... as early as 4z.

Winds should turn clockwise to north-northeast to northeast by 
early tomorrow afternoon. Tomorrow will be another day with a 
TEMPO and VCSH starting at 20z for similar threats- gusty outflow winds
in excess of 35 kts, rain, and briefly lowering ceilings. Ceilings
could briefly drop to around 7000 feet AGL given more mid-level 
moisture is expected to be present. A PRO30 or TEMPO will likely 
be needed past 0z Tuesday in the next update.

&&

.BOU WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Denver/Boulder CO
148 PM MDT Sun Aug 30 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Scattered showers and storms capable of producing strong to
  severe wind gusts are expected to continue through the evening. 

- Better precipitation chances on Monday, with another round of
  afternoon/evening showers and storms, a few may become severe.

- Warmer and drier conditions expected from Tuesday onward. 
  


&&

.DISCUSSION /Through Sunday/...
Issued at 124 PM MDT Sun Aug 30 2026

Current radar shows storms are making their way off the northern 
Front Range early this afternoon, with another round moving across 
the Continental Divide. The primary hazard with today's showers and 
storms will, once again, be strong outflow winds. So far, storms 
have been producing a few tenths of rainfall and wind gusts between 
40 to 50 mph. Storms have been moving between 30-40 kts, which will 
help keep flash flooding concerns limited, but if we do see any back-
building, there is enough moisture in place to see some heavy 
downpours, mainly across the higher elevations. While today's 
instability is expected to be slightly increased over Saturday, it
remains fairly weak, with only a few hundred to roughly 500 J/kg 
of MLCAPE observed on the SPC mesoanalysis. CAMs continue to be in
decent agreement about high-based storms/showers continuing their
trek eastward across the plains through the afternoon and 
evening. These will be capable of producing strong outflow winds, 
with at least a few severe wind gusts possible. Current 
temperature readings show roughly a ten degree difference from 
this time yesterday, with today's afternoon highs forecast to run 
a few degrees cooler than yesterday. 

Southwesterly flow aloft will continue to usher monsoonal moisture 
into Colorado on Monday. Given the increased moisture, proximity to 
the right entrance of a 500 mb jet, and the aid of lift from an 
approaching shortwave sometime in the afternoon/evening, this will 
be our best chance for precipitation across the forecast area 
with this wave of monsoonal moisture. CAMs continue to show a 
cluster of storms move through the Four Corners Monday morning, 
pushing northeast across Colorado through the day. We could see a 
few stronger to severe storms in the afternoon, with the CAMs 
honing in on the better instability being along and east of the 
Palmer Divide (as high as ~1200 J/kg of MLCAPE). Given the better 
moisture, we will have a better chance for some localized heavier 
rainfall amounts, but with the mean flow aloft roughly moving 
35-40 kts, this should help limit flash flood potential. 
Additionally, with DCAPE ranging from 1200-1500 J/kg across the 
plains, generally east of the urban corridor, the primary threat 
will be with gusty outflows once again, but with increasing 0-6 km
bulk shear, we may see some marginally severe hail with some of 
the stronger storms. Depending on the timing of the shortwave, we 
could see showers/storms linger late into the night. Near normal 
temperatures are expected across the forecast area. 

Southwesterly flow aloft will remain in place through the week as 
the upper-level ridge persists over the eastern US. Monsoonal 
moisture is expected to continue flowing into the region, but 
amounts are expected to diminish for a few days midweek, as the 
higher amounts should stay to our southeast. Things in the Pacific 
look to become active over this period, from a parade of storms 
moving towards Hawaii, to a fairly strong closed low dropping south 
along the West Coast. Depending on how these features interact, we 
could see some more active weather return by late in the week, but 
for now, the forecast calls for slightly less convection each 
afternoon after Monday, with near normal temperatures on Tuesday, 
gradually warming through the end of the work-week.  

&&

&&

.AVIATION /00Z TAFS through 00Z Tuesday/...
Issued at 545 PM MDT Sun Aug 30 2026

Radar as of 2345z is rather quiet across the Denver metro after 
an afternoon of showers, thunderstorms, and gusty winds at all 
three sites. CAMs continue to suggest the possibility of 
additional high-based showers and thunderstorms either moving off 
the Palmer Divide or the higher terrain to the west this evening 
through 5z. These could bring gusty outflow winds in excess of 35 
kts and briefly lowering ceilings. Behind the convection, winds 
will shift to drainage through Monday morning.

Winds should turn clockwise to north-northeast or even east by 
early tomorrow afternoon. Have continued to refine the timing of 
showers/thunderstorms for tomorrow afternoon and evening based on 
the latest CAMs. A TEMPO and VCTS starts at 21z (20z for KAPA) for
similar threats to today- gusty outflow winds in excess of 35 
kts and briefly lowering ceilings. Ceilings could briefly drop to
around 7000 feet AGL given more mid-level moisture than today is 
expected to be present. A PROB30 is in place for tomorrow evening 
with additional rounds of SHRA/TSRA possible. Timing of the 
SHRA/TSRA will continue to be refined in future updates.


&&

.BOU WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

.DISCUSSION /Through Sunday/...
Issued at 215 AM MDT Mon Aug 31 2026

SW flow aloft will continue today thru tonight.  Water vapor 
imagery shows one disturbance over nrn CO tonight which will move 
away from the area this morning. Meanwhile, a secondary 
disturbance embedded in the flow will move from nern AZ across wrn
CO late this aftn/early evening and into WY by late 
evening/overnight. There will continue to be an influx of monsoon 
moisture across the area with PW values up to 150% above normal. 
Thus will see showers/tstms become likely by mid to late aftn over
the higher terrain. Across the plains, MLCAPE will be around 1000
j/kg with bulk shear up to 30 kts. Overall, there will be some 
threat of wet microbursts from the stronger storms along with 
marginal large hail. Best timing of tstms will be from late aftn 
thru the mid evening hours. Storms will produce locally heavy rain
in some areas but they will be moving along as flow aloft 
increases this evening. As for highs, readings will be near 
seasonal normals.

On Tue, there will be a lingering chc of showers across the area in 
the morning hours.  By aftn, drier air in SW flow aloft will move 
into the area which will lead to lower chances for showers/tstms. 
Highs will remain near seasonal normals.

For Wed and Thu, dry air in SW flow aloft will remain over the area 
with only a low chc for aftn showers/tstms.  Temperatures will be 
warmer as readings rise into the upper 80's to lower 90s across the 
plains.

By Fri thru next weekend, an upper level high build over the central 
US as an upper level low resides over the Pacific NW.  This will 
allow for the flow aloft to become more SSW.  Models eventually want 
to advect some monsoon moisture, from the swrn US, into the higher 
terrain by the weekend.  If that happens then there would be an 
increasing chc for showers/tstms, mainly over the higher terrain. 
Across the plains, expect above normal temps to continue with just a 
slight chc of tstms next weekend.

&&

Issued at 1111 PM MDT Sun Aug 30 2026

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...A cool and wet start to meteorological fall. Some 
rain could be heavy, leading to poor drainage flooding.

The backdoor cold front that pushed southwest of New England this 
morning starts to shift back to the northeast today, with increasing 
cloud cover this afternoon. As advertised the past several days, 
there are multiple rounds of beneficial rainfall this week, with the 
first round coming late tonight through Tuesday. With the frontal 
boundary shifting northeast, PWATs increase to between 1.8-2.0 
inches, interacting with a weak wave of low pressure riding along 
the boundary.

Timing-wise, rain aims to arrive around midnight west of the CT 
River Valley and around the time of the Tuesday morning commute for 
the I-95 corridor. Looking at BUFKIT, do see warm rain processes 
with the warm cloud layer around 10k feet. Locally heavy downpours, 
especially during the daytime Tuesday, are possible, which may lead 
to localized street and poor drainage flooding. This coincides with 
the Day 1-2 ERO Marginal Risk (level 1 out of 4) for excessive 
rainfall.

Do think there will be a thin axis of heaviest rainfall across the 
southwest section of our CWA. Rainfall amounts are in the 
neighborhood of half an inch to an inch, with lesser amounts east of 
I-95, where totals are in the range of a quarter to half an inch. 
Since these are showers versus stratiform rain, there could be areas 
of higher and lower amounts within a relatively short distance. 
However, a subtle shift northeast could put some of the heaviest 
rainfall across parts of central Massachusetts and eastern 
Connecticut. Additionally, there's a lower chance for thunder, 
mainly Tuesday afternoon, with a few hundred J/kg of CAPE across 
mainly western Massachusetts and Connecticut, although it's not a 
significant risk.

Rain tapers off late Tuesday, with drier conditions overspreading 
the region Tuesday night into early Thursday morning. Given the 
clouds, expect a much cooler start to Tuesday, with highs mainly in 
the upper 60s to lower 70s. A true nod to the first day of 
meteorological fall.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Unsettled weather late Wed into Thursday, with 
several rounds of showers and thunderstorms. Low confidence on exact 
timing. 

1025 mb high pressure over the Maritimes should provide dry weather 
much of Wed, especially across eastern MA, while a frontal boundary 
lurks to the west and southwest of SNE. This front will eventually 
move northeast as a warm front later Wed and especially Wed night, 
resulting in an increased risk for showers and thunderstorms across 
SNE late Wed/Wed night. Cooler temps Wed, with 1025 Maritime high 
and ESE onshore flow, limiting max temps in the upper 60s and lower 
70s.

Trailing/secondary short wave and associated cold front impact the 
region around Thu. Potential for thunderstorms to become strong to 
severe during this time, as warm sector airmass overspreads SNE. 
However, better instability/higher theta-e airmass appears to remain 
southwest of SNE. Thus, potential for severe weather and flash 
flooding here looks limited at this time range. Heat and humidity 
return Thu with warm sector airmass, highs in the lower 80s and dew 
pts in the upper 60s and lower 70s. 

  
KEY MESSAGE 3...Improving weather Friday and into the holiday 
weekend. Other than a spot diurnal shower each day, dry weather 
prevails with a mix of clouds and sun. Cooler than normal with highs 
in the 70s and lows in the 50s, along with onshore breezes.

Definitely a sign of fall approaching, with robust northern stream 
Friday yielding a baroclinic 998 mb maritime low late Fri/Sat. This 
will yield a cool, brisk NE flow into the SNE over the weekend. 
Highs likely remaining in the 70s and overnight lows in the 50s. It 
will feel even cooler over southeast MA, including Cape Cod and the 
Islands, with northeast winds 15-25 mph. Cool cyclonic flow aloft 
will yield diurnal clouds each day and possibly a spot shower. 
Otherwise, dry weather prevails. Possibly warmer and less wind for 
Memorial Day Monday, as high amplitude trough moves offshore and 
1025 mb high settles over SNE.

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1: Diurnal thunderstorms expected through this 
weekend with the main threat of locally heavy rainfall.

A lingering outflow boundary was a focus of earlier showers and
likely will be again a focus for diurnally induced convection 
this afternoon and evening. Mesoanalysis reveals a strong 
gradient in PWATs from around 1.6 inches in the Piedmont to 
around 2.1 inches in the Coastal Plain. Expect scattered 
convection to develop with continued daytime heating in a 
moderately unstable environment but weak shear. Convection 
likely to favor the eastern Midlands and Coastal Plain where 
deeper moisture exists and aided by convergence along the sea 
breeze. DCAPE values are poor as are lapse rates so not 
expecting much of a severe threat, but with elevated PWATs and 
weak storm motion, heavy rain remains the primary threat with 
high rain rates possible. WPC continues to outlook the area in a
marginal risk of excessive rainfall. Little change Sunday in 
the overall pattern, although the upper trough axis will be 
weakening as the upper ridge to the west begins to expand 
eastward. Isolated diurnal convection remains possible given 
abundant atmospheric moisture in place. 

KEY MESSAGE 2: Well above normal temperatures expected with 
dangerous heat index values possible next week.

Increasing confidence in a hot and humid start to the month of 
September. Ensembles are in good agreement showing an anomalous 
upper ridge gradually migrating eastward from the MS Valley 
early in the week to the Appalachians and Carolinas by mid-late 
week. ESAT values of 500mb heights are above the 97th percentile
Monday and above the 99th percentile through mid week and 
remaining above the 90th percentile through the end of the week.
The strong upper ridging will create strong subsidence over the
region which should really limit convection much of the week. 
The result should be well above normal temperatures and this is 
supported by ensemble forecast temperatures at 700/850/1000mb at
or above the 99th percentile with EC EFI values for both max 
and min temperatures in the 0.7-0.8 range with non-zero shift of
tails. Highs expected to be in the mid to upper 90s with lows 
in the lower to mid 70s with little spread among the NBM IQR. 
The combination of above normal temperatures and increased low 
level moisture will yield high probabilities of heat indices in 
the 100-105 range and possibly higher.

strong 596DM upper ridge currently over the southern Plains and 
mid MS Valley area building eastward through the week becoming 
situated over the southern OH Valley and Carolinas by mid week 
then gradually weakening and beginning to slowly retrograde by 
the end of the week. This should result in strong subsidence 
over the region through the week with ensemble forecast 700mb 
temperatures at the 99th percentile with values around +10C. 
These high values and the notable subsidence inversion at 700mb 
increases confidence in the general lack of convection expected.

the 90th percentile early in the week and at the 99th percentile
mid to late week suggesting a strong warming trend through the 
week with anomalously high temperatures (about 10 degrees above 
normal). Minimum temperatures also expected to be anomalously 
high with EC EFI showing values around 0.7-0.8 and a nonzero 
shift of tails (similar to the max temperatures) with values 
about 5 to 10 degrees above normal. Southeast to southwesterly 
surface flow through the week will keep the low level moisture 
in place resulting in heat indices rising above 100 degrees all 
week and approaching heat advisory criteria mid to late week. 

KEY MESSAGE 2. Active weather and decreasing temperatures 
possible next weekend.

Ensembles and global guidance in good agreement showing the 
strong upper ridge retrograding westward back over the Plains 
states allowing for upper troughing along the East Coast next 
weekend. This should support slightly cooling temperatures and 
also allow shortwave energy to dive down the back side of the 
retreating ridge, bringing increased chances of rainfall back to
the forecast area. Rainfall will be welcomed again after a long
hot and generally dry week ahead. 

KEY MESSAGE 3. Diurnal thunderstorms expected through this 
evening with the main threat of locally heavy rainfall.

Stratus clouds have transitioned to a stratocumulus deck as 
daytime heating continues and temperatures rise through the 80s.
Dewpoints are generally in the lower 70s and should support 
moderate instability as higher clouds are diminishing and more 
sun is expected. However, wind shear remains weak and organized 
convection is not anticipated. Hi-res guidance suggests isolated
convection through the afternoon into early evening favoring 
the eastern Midlands closer to the deeper moisture (PWATs around
2 inches) and better upper forcing along the coast (500mb 
vorticity). Due to slow storm motion and PWATs around 2 inches, 
heavy rainfall could be a concern for more intense storms 
providing high rain rates.

western New Mexico, with the ridge axis continuing to translate 
east toward the Southern Plains through Sunday. By Sunday 
afternoon, the center of the ridge should be positioned near 
Oklahoma, placing North and Central Texas beneath increasingly 
strong subsidence and reinforcing the hot and predominantly dry 
pattern. One exception may be across southern and eastern Central 
Texas this afternoon, where lingering low-level moisture and 
strong heating should support modest instability along the 
northwestern edge of the more favorable moisture plume. If a weak 
convergence axis or subtle moisture discontinuity can develop, an 
isolated shower may briefly form, though probabilities remain 
around 10% or less and most locations will remain dry. 

Otherwise, efficient daytime mixing will again be the main 
forecast challenge. Observations continue to show afternoon 
dewpoints mixing lower than the NBM, with drier air entrained into
the boundary layer while increasingly dry soils limit evaporative
cooling. This favors more efficient, sensible heating and allows 
the mixed layer to tap into the warmer air aloft, resulting in a 
forecast that is hotter but less humid than the unmodified blend. 
Temperatures should reach the lower 100s across much of North 
Texas, with a few locations in the Metroplex and Big Country 
approaching 103-104 degrees. Despite the heat, lower afternoon 
dewpoints will keep apparent temperatures fairly close to the 
ambient temperature through Sunday, precluding the need for heat 
headlines this weekend.

Issued at 126 PM CDT Sat Aug 29 2026

The 594 dam subtropical ridge that dominated the Southern Plains 
over the weekend will continue shifting east toward the Midwest 
and Mid-Mississippi Valley through Tuesday. While the ridge 
remains the primary influence locally today, its eastward 
migration will gradually open the door for deeper Gulf moisture to
spread inland from the southeast. Today should therefore be the 
final largely uncomplicated hot and dry day across North and 
Central Texas, with highs near or above 100 degrees across much of
the region. Afternoon dewpoints continue to mix lower than 
blended guidance, keeping heat indices relatively close to the 
ambient temperature. Combined with very dry fuels and low 
afternoon humidity, elevated fire weather concerns will continue, 
especially across western North Texas. 

Potential Tropical Cyclone Five will approach the Upper Texas
coast Tuesday while moving around the southern periphery of the
ridge. Direct impacts from the system will remain well southeast
of the forecast area through the short term period, but increasing
southeasterly flow will begin drawing deeper moisture into Central
and East Texas. Rain chances will consequently increase across our
southeastern counties Tuesday afternoon, with the better coverage
still expected southeast of the CWA through the daytime hours.
Increasing humidity will push heat indices upward, but the
coverage and duration of advisory level values remain too limited
for a headline at this time. 

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Tuesday night through next Sunday)
Issued at 155 PM CDT Mon Aug 31 2026

The more notable forecast change occurs Tuesday night into 
Wednesday as the tropical system moves inland and weakens. This
will not be a complete breakdown of the upper ridge, but rather a
localized weakness moving northward around its western periphery.
Global deterministic and ensemble guidance generally support a 
northwestward and eventually northward turn of the remnant system,
though confidence remains lower in how long a coherent 
circulation survives inland. Some solutions maintain a weak 
remnant low or vorticity maximum into eastern North and Central 
Texas, resulting in a notable northwestward expansion of rain 
chances compared to previous forecasts. Southeasterly low-level 
flow would transport deeper moisture inland while weak convergence
and ascent near the remnant circulation reduce inhibition and 
make showers and thunderstorms less dependent on peak daytime 
heating. Accordingly, rain chances increase Tuesday night and 
Wednesday across eastern Central Texas and spread into eastern 
North Texas, including at least parts of the DFW Metroplex. 

Locally heavy rainfall will be possible where deeper tropical 
moisture overlaps the remnant circulation, particularly across the
southeastern counties, although the greater flooding threat 
should remain closer to Southeast Texas. The other meaningful 
impact will be on temperatures. Increasing humidity alone would 
favor higher heat indices, but greater cloud cover and scattered 
convection should hold daytime temperatures several degrees lower 
across eastern portions of the area Wednesday. This competing 
influence is one reason confidence in heat headline coverage 
decreases after Tuesday despite the increasingly humid air mass. 
Rain chances should gradually decrease Wednesday night into 
Thursday, but the exact timing will depend on how quickly the 
remnant circulation weakens. A faster dissipating system would 
allow rain to end sooner and temperatures to rebound, while a 
slower solution would maintain clouds and scattered convection 
across eastern portions of the area into Thursday. 

By late week and the Labor Day weekend, the tropical influence 
should diminish and attention will return to the subtropical 
ridge. Guidance differs on its exact position and strength, but 
the prevailing ensemble signal continues to favor above normal 
temperatures across North and Central Texas. Most areas should 
return to predominantly dry conditions Friday into the weekend as 
ridging becomes the stronger influence once again, though 
confidence in the details decreases with time.

Issued at 1103 PM CDT Fri Aug 28 2026

The very weak sfc low to our east will try to organize later today
into Sunday. This action will do two things, one...it will bring
drier dew pts down today due to the northerly flow on its west 
side. Second...the low will begin to slowly move west late today 
which will bring higher moisture content and storms back to the 
area as the eastern portion of the broad circulation reaches the 
area Sunday. This will be noticeable as dew pts move from the low 
to upper 60s today into the 70s by early Sunday. This will set up 
an environment for heavy rainfall producing storms, waterspouts 
and strong downbursts. Downbursts and damaging wind speeds with 
these storms should be mainly located nearest the retreating dry 
air mass. Storm motion will be toward land as well starting Sunday 
which could help bring a weak waterspout onshore. A weak tornado
developing inland wouldn't be ruled out either. The upper level 
flow is what we will be looking at to see if this thing will be 
able to gain any real strength since all other variables are in
its wheelhouse. The large high out west and the Bermuda high to 
the east will both be responsible for developing an upper low from
the current upper trough that is currently moving through the 
eastern half of the country. The Bermuda high will remain in place
causing the trough to slow and stall later today into Sunday. The
SW CONUS high will begin to ridge to the east and this will begin
to sharpen the trough quite a bit, eventually cutting off an 
upper low from the southern portion of the trough by Sunday. The 
upper low will move west along with the weak sfc low and depending
on where the sfc low is relative to the upper low, will determine
if the sfc low can strengthen which at this time looks to be too 
close to the upper low causing a lot of shear over the system. But
there is some possible pulsing regardless as the weak low moves 
into SE LA or along the coast. This low will eventually move WNW 
and we will be back to daily hit and miss storms as moisture 
profiles will have recovered with help from the east side of the 
low. Eventhough the hurricane center has this area with a 10% 
chance of being a cyclone, it will be a tough go for this to 
deepen that fast or to the extent it becomes a tropical cyclone 
problem. But the rainfall and strong storms associated with it 
could still cause issues for those impacted. Although the one 
nearest our area is not as worrisome for becoming a tropical 
cyclone, there is one that needs to be monitored over the coming 
days. The hurricane center is not showing this yet. But the open 
wave around 28N 68.5W will continue moving west while the remnants
of Dolly will be moving into the Bahamas around the same time. 
The remnants of Dolly and this open wave begin to combine as they 
move toward the FL east coast Tuesday. This area will need to be 
watched since the next destination could become the gulf.

down to the east-southeast over the southern Appalachians and 
towards the Atlantic coast while still stretching back through the 
mid MS Valley and possibly even back southwest towards northwestern 
Mexico. This places the Lower MS Valley and northern Gulf coast in a 
little of a weakness or possibly straight southeasterly to east-
southeasterly flow as the area remains on the periphery of the

continue to pump into the region. This is about 5-8 days away so

leading the the location of any heavy rain being displaced 
significantly. /CAB/

.SHORT TERM...
(Now through Tuesday)
Issued at 1230 PM CDT Sat Aug 29 2026

Weak low pressure located over the northern Gulf will continue to
meander westward through the remainder of the weekend. NHC
continues to indicate a VERY LOW (10%) chance of development with
this circulation. However, regardless of development, it will
bring scattered showers and thunderstorms to SE LA and S MS 
Sunday as it moves through the local area. 

Overall threat of severe weather looks low, but one or two storms
could still become strong to severe, mainly across western
portions of the area where drier mid level air will still be in 
place as the more humid air mass moves in from the east. For
comparison, forecast soundings near New Orleans indicate DCAPE of
around 500-600 J/kg while it's near or over 1000 J/kg near Baton
Rouge. 

Overall coverage should remain generally scattered, but a few of
the storms that do develop could result in a localized heavy rain
threat as a plume of deep tropical moisture moves westward with 
the low. Highest precipitable values will be located generally 
south of the I-10/12 corridor, where the model forecast soundings
indicate PW of 2.2-2.3" by midday. With those values being around
the 90th percentile for this time of year, some of the storms 
will be capable of efficient rainfall processes and would expect 
to see some high instantaneous rainfall rates. The saving grace, 
will be that storms should be moving generally 10-20 mph which 
should limit the amount of time any storm spends in one location. 
For the time being the area remains outlooked with a marginal 
threat of excessive rainfall/flash flooding, and this seems 
reasonable based on the storm motions. Will be watching for any 
signs of multiple storms moving over a given area in quick 
succession, which would lead to a locally increased threat.

The weak low will be slow to move away from the area as upper 
level high pressure builds into the middle Mississippi Valley and 
serves to weaken the steering flow. It will continue to gradually 
shift westward through the first part of the work week, though the
local air mass will remain quite humid with PW values generally 
in the 1.9-2" range, or around the 75th percentile. With the 
strongest ridging forecast to remain north of the local area, the
combination of deep moisture and daytime heating should result in
scattered to numerous showers and storms Monday and Tuesday.

Regarding temperatures, cloud cover and convection should keep
afternoon temperatures in check, but with dewpoints forecast in
the mid to upper 70s, heat index values could still approach 
advisory conditions before convection begins firing.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Tuesday Night through Friday) 
Issued at 1230 PM CDT Sat Aug 29 2026

The second half of the work week brings more of the same as an
active weather pattern persists. Multiple weak disturbances look
to move toward the area, though there is quite a bit of spread in
the exact timing and specific details of each one. 

The first disturbance is currently located near southern Florida
and may completely dissipate before reaching the local area. 
However, if it does not, it would arrive some time Tuesday night
into Wednesday morning. It's also possible this disturbance may be
absorbed by a second disturbance following closely on its heels.
That one looks to bring another plume of increased moisture to the
local area during the Wednesday into Thursday time frame. 

And finally, another disturbance (the moisture associated with the
remnants of TS Dolly) could be moving into the northeastern Gulf
by late Friday, possibly approaching the local area by Saturday.

None of these disturbances currently look to be significant
threats as far as tropical development is concerned. But
regardless of that, will need to monitor each disturbance and the
potential for at least localized heavy rain as the associated deep
moisture will continue to allow for efficient rainfall processes 
in some storms.

.SHORT TERM...
(Now through Wednesday night)
Issued at 1051 PM CDT Sat Aug 29 2026

No big changes from the ongoing fcast as wet periods look to be
the future of this coming week. The rain and storms that will move
into the area won't be continuous but instead in waves. This will
be from a deep fetch of tropical moisture moving in with PW values
2.2+" which will drop back into the upper 1.8 to 2.0 range in
between. The current sfc low in the north central gulf is 
interacting with the base of an upper long wave trough which can
be seen very well in WV imagery this morning. It is currently
moving west and this will be the first of 2+" PWs that we see as
the area gets into the east side of the sfc low. The low is
expected to remain weak while interacting with the upper trough
and eventual upper low cutting off from the trough base today.
But, as the sfc low moves west just offshore the Louisiana coast,
the upper level winds weaken and conditions become slightly more
favorable as move into Monday and Tuesday. The next surge looks to
visit late Tue into Wed which would be the mess seen off the east
coast of Florida this morning. The area even farther out to the
east of the "mess" will be the next which should partner up with 
the remnants of Dolly as it moves near the east coast of Florida 
Wed. Regardless of the several disturbances that move into the 
gulf over the coming days, conditions are not primed for rapid 
development of tropical activity, but fcasts can and do change. At
the moment, we definitely see deep slugs of tropical moisture 
making its way into our area through mid week, but unless shear
values drop aloft, the trend will remain for low probs of tropical
development.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Thursday night through Saturday night)
Issued at 1051 PM CDT Sat Aug 29 2026

Overall the medium range models and ensembles are still 
in agreement with an active pattern continuing through next weekend. 
All guidance suggest the mid lvl ridge builds east with the center 
of it working all the way into the the Tobacco Road region before 
the stalls.  The ridge will be setup in a way that puts the local 
area and the northwestern Gulf on the southwestern periphery of the 
ridge which will allow for multiple tropical waves/disturbances to 
impact the region. NBM for the most part matches what the medium 
range guidance is suggesting however there are still subtle timing 
and placement issues and because of that we will not make any major 
deviations from the latest NBM.  

By Wednesday night the ridge will be firmly situated to the north 
and northeast allowing for southeasterly flow over the northwestern 
Gulf coast. Easterly waves will work underneath the ridge as they 
move into the Gulf and then slide towards the northwest. Again there 
are some timing discrepancies by the next tropical after our 
Sunday/Monday system could be as early as overnight Tuesday or as 
late as early Thursday. The low lvl feature could approach earlier 
but looking at the moisture field and PWs it appears that would try 
to surge into the area late Wednesday and overnight. 

The next feature to focus on appears to be the remnants of Dolly. 
Dolly is currently just east of the Lesser Antilles and should 
impact Puerto Rico in the next 24 hours with hopefully some much 
needed rainfall. Then it will continue to move west-northwest into 
the Gulf late in the work week and with the ridge still in place 
with southeast flow aloft those remnants could approach the region 
late Friday and into Saturday. 

Both of these features much like the current one in the Gulf don't 
look to promising from a tropical development stand point but all 
look to bring rain and possibly heavy rain at times. Moisture will 
be abundant and the rain will be very efficient and if things line 
up in an unwanted way we could see the potential for multiple heavy 
rain events. We will need to closely monitor these waves over the 
next few days. Now as mentioned earlier this will be highly dictated 
by placement of the ridge, track of the any of these waves, and 
timing and it would not be a surprising to see quite the dichotomy 
across the region where the southwestern portions of the CWA see 
multiple inches of rain and possibly on multiple days where the 
northern and northeastern portions of the CWA see less than an inch 
overall with highs possibly in mid 90s. /CAB/

.SHORT TERM...
(Now through Wednesday night)
Issued at 1225 PM CDT Sun Aug 30 2026

Upper ridge centered north of Dallas this morning. An upper 
disturbance was off the southeast Louisiana coast to the south of 
Grand Isle. Surface high was over Virginia. Scattered showers and a 
few thunderstorms were rotating around the upper disturbance,
mainly over the coastal waters this morning, but are becoming 
more numerous over land this afternoon, mainly along and south of
the Interstate 10/12 corridor. Temperatures are approaching 90,
but probably won't get much higher than they are now. 

The disturbance over the Gulf is expected to drift slowly west or 
west-northwest over the next couple of days, likely reaching the 
upper Texas coast on Tuesday. Another disturbance will enter the 
eastern Gulf on Wednesday. Precipitable water values between 1.9 
and 2.1 inches are expected over much of the area through 
Wednesday. These are generally between the 75th and 90th 
percentile climatologically, and are more than sufficient to 
produce scattered to numerous showers and storms across the area. 
The best areal coverage is expected over the southern half of the 
area from the Interstate 10/12 corridor to the coast today and
again on Monday. The disturbance may be far enough away from the 
area Tuesday to limit areal coverage as compared to the next 36 
hours. Rainfall amounts each day will be highly variable, with 
only very limited areas getting heavy rainfall (> 1 inch). If
those spots of heavy rainfall occur over an urban area, they could
cause temporary problems, but widespread flooding issues are not
anticipated. Most of the precipitation should occur during the 
hours of maximum heating (afternoon), with much or all of the 
precipitation dissipating near or shortly after sunset each day.
The exception would be along immediate coastal areas, such as the
lower portions of the Louisiana coastal parishes, which could see
showers return near or before sunrise. 

Forecast soundings support highs in the 90 to 95 degree range 
through Wednesday. In most cases, those highs will be around midday 
or early afternoon, before convection becomes widespread. Areas 
that see convection develop early could even fall short of 90 
degrees each day. 

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Thursday through Saturday night)
Issued at 1225 PM CDT Sun Aug 30 2026

The disturbance over the eastern Gulf on Wednesday is expected to 
track westward along the northern Gulf Coast Thursday and Friday, 
and be very close to Lake Pontchartrain at that point, before 
weakening or dissipating. The remnants of former Tropical Storm 
Dolly are expected to enter the far southeastern Gulf by Friday, 
with disagreement on what happens beyond that point. 

Not seeing any indications of significant drying or subsidence in at 
least the global operational runs through next weekend, so we'll be 
carrying precipitation in the forecast each day. Not a lot of 
variance between the global temperature guidance, so no real targets 
of opportunity to make adjustments from the NBM.

carbon copy of today regarding precipitation timing, coverage and
impacts.

.SHORT TERM...
(Now through Thursday night)
Issued at 1050 PM CDT Sun Aug 30 2026

Very compact tropical system at roughly 215 miles due south of New
Orleans this morning. These type of systems can develop rapidly
due to their small size so its possible that it can deepen enough
to bring it to cyclone status later today since all variables are
hospitable for its development. The system has no immediate 
impacts expected inland on this side of the state but as it moves 
WNW, it will eventually have impacts for the west side. Marine 
areas will be the only real impacts locally and most if not all of
that will be well offshore. The system will provide a continued 
weakness over the area with onshore flow keeping precip numbers 
elevated today and this higher coverage should remain through much
of this week as a deep layered tropical flow should continue. The
majority of this week will be a rather diurnal pattern playing 
out with daytime storms and not a lot of activity overnight inland
and a temporal opposite of that for marine areas. The next two 
systems that would highten rain/storm chances are still embedded 
in this deep easterly flow and timing of those are still intact. 
These can easily be seen in any sat imagery with the first being 
just east of the Florida east coast and the second at around 28N 
72W. The second one is the most questionable at this time and is 
stationary at the moment. Models want to bring it closer to the 
east coast of Florida by Tue then slow it to a stall as it feels 
the east coast trough. Then what occur with the remnants of Dolly,
does it assimilate with this disturbance or does it remain 
seperate? The answers to these will eventually be solved, but for 
now, they are valid questions. The area off the east coast of 
Florida becomes quite conducive for development over the coming 
days. So, to see something eventually develop over that area would
not be surprising.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Thursday night through Sunday) 
Issued at 1050 PM CDT Sun Aug 30 2026

The overall thinking in the extended portion of the forecast 
hasn't changed much with an active setup through the week. 
However, noticed some indications last night and there is 
definitely a trend in the medium range guidance and associated 
ensemble means towards the pattern changing as we move into next 
weekend. This shift is towards a more typical late summer setup 
with the ridge building and more centered of the plains. Thus a 
drier and warmer forecast especially late next weekend and heading
into the first full week of September. With much of the forecast 
focused on the current system just south of our coast and another 
possible tropical wave moving in around the middle part of the 
week along with a lower confidence forecast for Friday and through
next weekend we will stick with the latest NBM. This still has 
above normal PoPs for much of the area both Friday and Saturday 
but then we see PoPs start to drop. 

The main key in the extended forecast is the evolution of the mid 
lvl ridge. B late Thursday The ridge will be dominating much of the 
Mid MS Valley across the southern Appalachians while the ridge axis 
stretches from northwestern/north-central Mexico across the TN 
Valley and into the Atlantic off of the Carolina coast. Then 
beginning overnight Thursday and especially Friday the ridge begins 
to strengthen to our northwest while still wrapping back around over 
the southeastern CONUS. This could be a little worrisome as we could 
see our next tropical wave, which is expected to move into the 
north-central and northwestern Gulf mid week, possibly get trapped 
under/blocked by the ridge somewhere over eastern TX and western LA. 
If and where that occurs it could become a potential heavy rain 
producer for the back half of the week. And this heavy rain could 
fall over some areas that possibly just saw heavy rain with the 
current tropical disturbance just to our south. That is not all, as 
the remnants of TS Dolly is expected to continue to move west and 
will begin to move into the Gulf late this week, possibly overnight 
Friday and early Saturday. However, there is a lot of uncertainty of 
with this. 

As was mentioned last night this forecast is highly dependent on the 
location of the ridge and timing of the next wave.  We will need to 
closely monitor these waves over the next few days. There is a good 
chance that we will have quite the QPF gradient over the region with 
northeastern 3rd/half being influenced by the ridge more thus 
leading to much lower rainfall totals possibly less than an inch 
total for the next 7 days. However, the southwestern 3rd/half just 
far enough on the periphery and seeing more impacts from our 
tropical disturbances and thus possible seeing multiple days where 
multiple inches of rain could fall and total rainfall could easily 
be over 3 to 5 inches in localized spots. /CAB/

.SHORT TERM...
(Now through Thursday night)
Issued at 1250 PM CDT Mon Aug 31 2026

Upper ridge was centered along the Arkansas-Missouri border this 
morning, with newly designated Tropical Depression Five (TD 5)  
about 130 miles south of Morgan City. To this point of the 
morning, convection over land in our area has been rather 
minimal, but do expect some uptick in areal coverage over the next
few hours. Temperatures generally 85 to 90 at noon CDT with dew 
points in the mid 70s.

Per NHC forecasts, TD 5 is expected to move away from the local 
area and reach the northwestern Gulf Coast on Tuesday. No major 
impacts are anticipated over our land areas today or tonight, 
although an increase in areal coverage of precipitation, compared 
to the present, is expected this afternoon. 

Center of upper ridge drifts slowly eastward over the next few days 
and will be along the Kentucky-Tennessee border on Thursday. Another 
weak low pressure is expected to be in the eastern Gulf at mid-week 
to the south of the upper ridge, but not a lot of agreement between 
the GFS and ECMWF as to how far west it may move in that time. 
Precipitable water values continue to run mainly between the 75th 
and 90th percentiles through Thursday, which should support 
scattered to numerous showers and storms over land each day with 
brief heavy downpours. Marginal risk of Excessive Rainfall is 
primarily in case those heavy downpours occur in sensitive (urban) 
areas. At least for now, antecedent conditions don't justify any 
need for watches. 

Highs likely to top out in the 90 to 95 degree range at most each
day, with convective temperatures not getting above that point. 
Did back off hourly dew points a degree or two during the day, as 
conditions and guidance don't support the NBM forecasts in the 
afternoons. Heat index values should remain just below advisory 
criteria.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Friday through Sunday night)
Issued at 1250 PM CDT Mon Aug 31 2026

Medium range models gradually rebuild the upper ridge westward over 
the weekend, with it centered over Kansas/Oklahoma by next Monday. 
Not a lot of agreement at this point regarding timing, strength or
location of any upper trough or surface low pressure moving 
across the local area south of the upper ridge. The operational 
global models would lean toward the ECMWF as a bit wetter 
solution, but neither would indicate any day as being completely 
dry, or a total washout. Any outdoor activities during the 
holiday weekend should plan for potential interruptions, but those
interruptions could be fairly brief.

No significant cooling anticipated over the next week. If
conditions end up a bit drier than anticipated, highs could again
get into the middle 90s over the weekend, which may necessitate
Heat Advisories.

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 231 PM CDT Sun Aug 30 2026

A shortwave disturbance over northeastern Iowa will continue to
drive showers and embedded thunderstorms eastward through early
this evening, with the greatest coverage expected north of 
I-80. While a 20% chance for lightning remains, poor mid-level 
lapse rates across northern Illinois should limit thunderstorms 
to isolated coverage.

Following the eastward departure of this short-wave impulse 
this evening, a southwesterly low-level jet will ramp up again 
overnight, with the core expected to reside over IA 
northeastward into southern WI. Associated isentropic upglide 
(warm air advection) may thus foster more isolated to scattered 
showers and thunderstorms late tonight into early Monday 
morning. Thereafter, capping is likely to curtail the threat of 
convection for much of the area into Monday afternoon. However, 
another short-wave impulse is progged to translate eastward 
towards northwestern IL late in the day, and thus may act as the
impetus for isolated to widely scattered afternoon development 
across northwestern IL after 2 pm. Should this activity occur, 
~40 kt of mid-level westerly flow could support a few stronger 
storms across northwestern IL late in the afternoon. Confidence 
remains low with the extent of this threat. 

Convective trends continue to be of low confidence Monday night
into Tuesday morning. Nevertheless, low (20-30%)chances for 
storms continue due to the persistent warm-air advection pattern
in combination with additional smaller scale perturbations 
likely to transition eastward across southern WI through the 
mid-level ridge axis. The better focus for storms may remain in 
southern WI, but at this time, cannot rule out storms as far 
south as the I-80 corridor. The SPC day 3 severe outlook (for 
Tuesday) places most areas north of I-80 in a level 1 of 5 
threat. So, while confidence in the coverage of storms remains 
low into Tuesday morning, the meteorological environment will be
supportive of a conditional threat for strong storms. 

Outside of the threat of storms through Tuesday morning, 
temperatures and humidity levels will be on the rise through 
mid-week as the airmass under the expansive mid/upper-level 
ridge continues to warm. We anticipate high temperatures in the 
upper 80s Monday, the low 90s Tuesday and the low to mid 90s 
Wednesday. In spite of us being past the peak timing for 
evapotranspiration, limited mixing under an inversion centered 
near 850 mb should keep dew points in the low to mid 70s during 
peak heating, particularly on Tuesday and Wednesday, resulting 
in peak heat indices in the 100 to 105 range. 

Relief from the heat looks plausible later in the week as a
backdoor cold front sags southward into the area. However, this
looks to come at the expense of a period of more active weather
(a period or two of thunderstorms, some possibly strong) at the
end of the week. The specifics such as the timing of the front
and best potential for thunderstorms remain a bit unclear at
this point, but storm chances begin to ramp up across our area
late Wednesday night into Thursday.

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 200 AM CDT Mon Aug 31 2026

Thunderstorms have fizzled out, but isolated showers fester over
the forecast area early this morning. Similar to last night, a
southwest to northeast low level jet (LLJ) is expected to
amplify prior to daybreak and help induce additional shower and
storm coverage. There is lower confidence on the exact 
coverage; but considering how impressive last night/yesterday 
morning's coverage ended up being, widely scattered showers and 
storms can be expected through daybreak before gradually 
diminishing (as the LLJ weakens) and moves east. Forcing becomes
fairly nebulous behind the LLJ. Most areas should receive a 
period of dry conditions around midday, but maintained slight 
chance PoPs for a stray diurnal shower that might pop-up this 
afternoon, mainly north of Interstate 88.

Stepping back and zooming out for a second, GOES IR and water 
vapor satellite imagery currently shows broad cloud cover 
sweeping across the CONUS from the Four Corners, to the 
Minnesota arrowhead, down to our nation's capital. Their 
movement is riding over an upper level ridge that has dominated 
the forecast for the last several days. IR is showing showers 
and storms over eastern Colorado/northwestern Kansas that is 
collocated with an upper level short wave embedded in the 
ridge. This wave is expected to quickly move across the Great 
Plains and head toward southwestern Wisconsin today. Model 
soundings are showing a fairly strong cap and a robust dry air 
over much of the area this afternoon and early evening with 
DCAPE values around 1000 J/kg in northwest Illinois. The cap 
might be enough to inhibit shower and storm development, but 
lapse rates are expected to steepen along with modest deep layer
shear with the arrival of the short wave. Any elevated storm 
that develops upstream strengthen and possibly produce some 
hail up to the size of a quarter or potentially localized 
damaging wind gusts, mainly for areas north of Interstate 88. 
The main bit of uncertainty is the exact track of the wave. If 
it follows the ridge, it could move right over northern 
Illinois, with favored areas closer to the Wisconsin stateline. 
But some models have a slightly more northern track into 
Wisconsin which would limit shower/storm coverage.

Even as the wave passes to the northeast, broad warm air
advection behind the wave could allow for festering showers once
again overnight into early Tuesday morning. For now, kept 
"silent" PoPs (10 to 14 percent chance) with no formal forecast 
mention, but trends will be monitored. At the risk of sounding 
like a broken record, but models are suggesting yet another 
wave embedded within the ridge is expected to pass nearby on 
Tuesday morning/early afternoon. However, models are showing a 
lot of disagreement with this wave. The NAM currently has the 
northernmost solution that may keep most of the forecast area 
dry, whereas the latest 00Z guidance is starting to bring that 
wave closer down into northern Illinois. With increasing 
instability ahead of the wave, it provides another chance where 
storms could become strong to severe. This also just highlights 
the pattern that the region currently finds itself in with 
persistent waves within the ridge pattern that keeps periodic 
shower/storm chances in the forecast. However, shower/storm 
chances on Tuesday could impact the temperature forecast.

As the upper level ridge slowly ambles east through midweek,
southwest winds are expected to advect in a warmer air mass and
higher dewpoints into the region. High temperatures are expected
to climb into the low 90s with dew point temperatures into the
low to possibly mid 70s. Models have been fairly consistent in
suggesting Wednesday could be the hottest day of the week where
heat index values could reach the mid to upper 90s for much of
the forecast area, and better chances that they could meet or 
exceed 100 south of Interstate 80. Confidence lowers in exact
heat values from south to north across the forecast area with
greatest uncertainty closer to the top of the ridge (north of
Interstate 80) given the better chances for showers and storms
there.

Models are suggesting that the ridge could break down by the 
end of the work week. That will help the hottest of temperatures
cool off a bit, but it will return the upper level flow pattern
to the northwest and thus bring with it additional chances for 
showers/storms toward and over the weekend.

Thunderstorms have fizzled out, but isolated showers fester over
the forecast area early this morning. Similar to last night, a
southwest to northeast low level jet (LLJ) is expected to
amplify prior to daybreak and help induce additional shower and
storm coverage. There is lower confidence on the exact 
coverage; but considering how impressive last night/yesterday 
morning's coverage ended up being, widely scattered showers and 
storms can be expected through daybreak before gradually 
diminishing (as the LLJ weakens) and moves east. Forcing becomes
fairly nebulous behind the LLJ. Most areas should receive a 
period of dry conditions around midday, but maintained slight 
chance PoPs for a stray diurnal shower that might pop-up this 
afternoon, mainly north of Interstate 88.

Stepping back and zooming out for a second, GOES IR and water 
vapor satellite imagery currently shows broad cloud cover 
sweeping across the CONUS from the Four Corners, to the 
Minnesota arrowhead, down to our nation's capital. Their 
movement is riding over an upper level ridge that has dominated 
the forecast for the last several days. IR is showing showers 
and storms over eastern Colorado/northwestern Kansas that is 
collocated with an upper level short wave embedded in the 
ridge. This wave is expected to quickly move across the Great 
Plains and head toward southwestern Wisconsin today. Model 
soundings are showing a fairly strong cap and a robust dry air 
over much of the area this afternoon and early evening with 
DCAPE values around 1000 J/kg in northwest Illinois. The cap 
might be enough to inhibit shower and storm development, but 
lapse rates are expected to steepen along with modest deep layer
shear with the arrival of the short wave. Any elevated storm 
that develops upstream strengthen and possibly produce some 
hail up to the size of a quarter or potentially localized 
damaging wind gusts, mainly for areas north of Interstate 88. 
The main bit of uncertainty is the exact track of the wave. If 
it follows the ridge, it could move right over northern 
Illinois, with favored areas closer to the Wisconsin stateline. 
But some models have a slightly more northern track into 
Wisconsin which would limit shower/storm coverage.

Even as the wave passes to the northeast, broad warm air
advection behind the wave could allow for festering showers once
again overnight into early Tuesday morning. For now, kept 
"silent" PoPs (10 to 14 percent chance) with no formal forecast 
mention, but trends will be monitored. At the risk of sounding 
like a broken record, but models are suggesting yet another 
wave embedded within the ridge is expected to pass nearby on 
Tuesday morning/early afternoon. However, models are showing a 
lot of disagreement with this wave. The NAM currently has the 
northernmost solution that may keep most of the forecast area 
dry, whereas the latest 00Z guidance is starting to bring that 
wave closer down into northern Illinois. With increasing 
instability ahead of the wave, it provides another chance where 
storms could become strong to severe. This also just highlights 
the pattern that the region currently finds itself in with 
persistent waves within the ridge pattern that keeps periodic 
shower/storm chances in the forecast. However, shower/storm 
chances on Tuesday could impact the temperature forecast.

As the upper level ridge slowly ambles east through midweek,
southwest winds are expected to advect in a warmer air mass and
higher dewpoints into the region. High temperatures are expected
to climb into the low 90s with dew point temperatures into the
low to possibly mid 70s. Models have been fairly consistent in
suggesting Wednesday could be the hottest day of the week where
heat index values could reach the mid to upper 90s for much of
the forecast area, and better chances that they could meet or 
exceed 100 south of Interstate 80. Confidence lowers in exact
heat values from south to north across the forecast area with
greatest uncertainty closer to the top of the ridge (north of
Interstate 80) given the better chances for showers and storms
there.

end of the work week. That will help the hottest of temperatures
cool off a bit, but it will return the upper level flow pattern
to the northwest and thus bring with it additional chances for 
showers/storms toward and over the weekend.

currently supporting an area of showers along the Nebraska and
Kansas borders. Broad west-southwesterly upper-level flow should
direct the wave toward the Lower Great Lakes this afternoon,

isolated to scattered shower and storm development this
afternoon focused near the Wisconsin state line. The inherited
PROB30 groups focused on the afternoon/evening period handle 
this nicely including implied uncertainties in coverage with
southward extent.

and generally weak (20-25kt) southwesterly low-level flow within
the humid regime may encourage a random shower or two to 
develop at any terminal through the overnight hours. Winds will 
be light (5 kt our less) out of the west to southwest.

develop and roll across northern Illinois after daybreak
Tuesday. The forecast outcome in which storms occur depends 
entirely on the coverage and intensity of storms that develop 
tonight (if at all) in the central Plains. At this point, there

round of thunder in the last 6 hours of the ORD/MDW TAF, but 
will brief the incoming shift on such a threat.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 247 PM CDT Mon Aug 31 2026

While we're about to turn the page on the calendar to 
meteorological fall, the weather pattern is much more 
reminiscent of mid-summer with a strong mid-upper level ridge of
high pressure from the central plains east to the mid-Atlantic.
Low amplitude shortwave troughs continue to ride along the 
flanks of this upper ridge, with one such wave responsible for 
the elevated showers and t-storms over northern Illinois this 
afternoon. Short range guidance has largely been performing 
poorly handling these small scale features and their associated 
convection, so the short term forecast was driven largely by 
extrapolating the shortwave eastward using water vapor imagery. 
The trough axis and associated forcing should be moving east to 
Lake Michigan early this evening, so would anticipate a decrease
in coverage of precip late this afternoon into early this 
evening from west to east. 

The next shortwave trough of interest is located over the 4 
corners region and should turn northeast and east around the 
western periphery of the ridge tonight into Tuesday. Guidance 
that has initialized this wave generally tracks it north of our 
CWA Tuesday afternoon as the upper ridge strengthens a bit over 
the mid-Mississippi Valley. An axis of very strong instability 
with minimal convective inhibition is expected from Iowa east 
into southern Wisconsin and far northern Illinois. CAM guidance,
which hasn't performed well lately, keeps convection with this 
feature focused mostly north of the IL/WI border. Despite what 
looks to be only a glancing shot of forcing with this shortwave,
we have opted to carry chance PoPs tomorrow afternoon near the 
WI border and Slight chace PoPs south to nearly I-80. If any 
mature convection can become established in this environment 
Tuesday afternoon, severe thunderstorms would be likely given 
the very strong instability and 30-40 kt of 0-6 km shear. 
Confidence remains low given the potential for the stronger 
forcing to remain north of the uncapped/strongly unstable air 
mass over our region. If it becomes clear that forcing will be 
sufficient for storms into our CWA (most likely northern CWA), 
then a substantially greater risk of severe thunderstorms would 
be likely.

The other big story is the late season heat and humidity. 
Pretty good agreement among the various models that 925 mb temps
in the mid to upper 20s Celsius will advect into the area 
Tuesday and Wednesday. This should support high temperatures in 
the lower to potentially mid 90s both afternoons, though the 
potential for convection/convective debris cloudiness leads to 
lower confidence in temperatures north of I-80. 

In addition to the heat, very humid conditions are expected 
with 70 degree dewpoints pooling from Iowa east across northern 
and central Illinois into Indiana. While we are past peak 
evapotranspiration (ET) season, climatologically ET in early 
September is not negligible and tends to be similar to what we 
typically see in mid-late June. Evidence of this ET was quite 
apparent today with dewpoints jumping 4-8F late this morning 
into early this afternoon from southern IA east into 
northern/central IL. Morning soundings suggest this jump in 
surface dewpoints wasn't the result of mixing down high moisture
and with lower dewpoints upstream, this jump wasn't from 
horizontal advection, strongly suggesting it was largely driven 
by ET. There is reason to be concerned that this ET could result
in dewpoints locally reaching the mid to even locally upper 70s
Tuesday/Wednesday afternoons, especially in the more heavily 
agricultural areas. 

The combination of high temperatures in the low to potentially mid 
90s and dewpoints in the 70s should result in peak afternoon heat 
indices of 100 to locally over 105 degrees. Opted to hoist a heat 
advisory for both Tuesday and Wednesday afternoon/early evenings for 
areas near/south of I-80 where confidence is highest in temps. If it 
becomes more apparent that cloud cover and/or convection won't 
hinder heating north of I-80, it is quite plausible that the heat 
advisory will need to be expanded north, especially Wednesday. While 
our currently forecasted heat indices are only approaching heat 
advisory criteria, we opted to issue an advisory anyway due to the 
potential for dewpoints/heat indices ending higher than forecast. 
Also, with schools back in session with outdoor activities and it 
having been weeks since we've seen heat indices over 100F, erring on 
the side of caution seemed warranted. 

As it looks now, the parade of ridge-rider shortwaves may push 
safely north of the area Wednesday, but by Thursday and Friday the 
upper ridge will begin to weaken and slowly shift westward. This 
could put our area back into the favorable track area for shortwaves 
bringing occasional showers/thunderstorm chances. This should also 
result in an easing of the more intense heat and humidity. Medium 
range guidance supports a continuation of an unsettled northwest 
flow pattern could support occasional chances for showers and 
thunderstorms into the upcoming weekend.

- Izzi

county. Low cloud coverage will increase Monday morning with the
falling hgts and increased onshore flow. The Central Coast, VTA
coast and LA coast will likely have good stratus coverage. The

.SHORT TERM (TDY-THU)...31/111 PM.

Multiple large troughs of low pressure will drive the weather 
through the week. The core of the energy and moisture will stay 
far enough to the north to not be concern with any rain or strong
winds, but it will maintain below normal temperatures. To clarify
however, with this being the hottest time of the year, below 
normal temperatures does not mean it is time to dust off the
jackets. It will still feel warm, but thankfully not hot like it 
was last week. Tropical moisture will stay away from the region as
well so it will also not feel as muggy as it did last week. With 
ocean temperatures still in the 70s however, it will still feel 
more humid than usual. 

A deep marine layer (2,000+ feet) will continue through the week 
as well, and should deepen a little more tomorrow as the trough
sags to the south. Would expect a spot or two to see drizzle in 
the morning where the clouds develop, especially near the Central
Coast foothills. Solid night through morning low clouds are most 
likely on the Central Coast, but coverage to the south should 
remain spotty thanks to the warmer ocean temperatures, despite the
marine layer being just as deep. It is impossible to predict
exactly where those random spots of clouds will form. 

Sundowner winds will continue each night over southwest Santa
Barbara County and flirt with an Advisory each time. Tonight looks
just under Advisory levels, while Tuesday and Wednesday night 
look just over.

.LONG TERM (FRI-MON)...31/140 PM.

Little change expected on Friday compared to the first half of the
week.

All eyes remain focused on the Labor Day holiday weekend period. A
Hurricane is likely to develop by Wednesday or Thursday from the 
clump of clouds currently just off the Baja coast. Once it forms,
it will likely move to the northwest through Saturday and towards
southern California. The big question is where will it head after
Saturday. Some deterministic models, like the current GFS, keeps 
the storm moving northward and right through southern California 
by Monday or Tuesday. Others, like the deterministic ECMWF, show 
the storm turning to the west and never even sniffing California. 
These are just two of many projections, but they do represent the
two extreme scenarios between a major rain and wind event and 
little to nothing. Peering into the ensemble solutions, they 
suggest that the heavy rain scenario is the least likely outcome 
(5-10% of the 100 projections have 2+ inches of rain). The 
completely dry scenario comprises 20-30% of the solutions. Which 
means in terms of rain, the most likely outcome is for some light
rain impacting the holiday weekend. The wind story is similar, 
with a low but non-zero chance of strong east winds causing fire 
and downed tree concerns. With all that said, this is definitely a
period to monitor with a range of outcomes on the table. Due to
the rarity of this storm, expecting there to be a lot of
uncertainty even as we get to the weekend, but hopefully some 
details will come more into focus by mid-week once the storm 
actually form. 

There is growing confidence for significant impacts at the coast
however. Unless the storm takes a full left turn after Saturday,
the south swell will be pumping through Tuesday, especially
considering the swells from the current Hurricane Karina also
still around. The evening high tides are also expected to be near
7 feet by Monday. The most likely scenario would result in high 
surf during a busy holiday weekend and moderate coastal flooding 
on south facing beaches. If the storm gets closer to the coast, 
those impacts will be amplified.

Issued at 403 AM EDT Sun Aug 30 2026

Model guidance remains consistent in depicting a rather wet pattern 
prevailing across SoFlo through the next several days. U/L high 
pressure is expected to remain over the SE CONUS, slowly migrating 
eastward. Meanwhile, the W Atl sfc ridge will remain just north of 
the state, allowing for a deep easterly wind regime to remain in 
place. This will keep supporting tropical moisture across the 
area, with afternoon sea breezes acting as focal points for deeper
convection. 

00Z MFL and model sounding data shows PWATs remaining in the 1.9-
2.3" range, while short-range model instability variables show 
CAPE/MUCAPE in the 2-3K J/kg range. At the same time, synoptic 
analyses depicts a Tropical Upper tropospheric Trough (TUTT) feature 
gradually lifting north from the Florida Keys through the rest of 
the peninsula today. Therefore, the combination of these key 
parameters plus the aforementioned moisture advection (along with
dew points in the upper 70s to around 80F) will result in max 
POPs of 70-80% each day. Potential for strong to severe storms is 
also anticipated, with wide-spread sea-breeze convection shifting 
inland through the evening hours. Main hazards will be frequent 
lightning, damaging wind gusts, and heavy rain. Localized flooding
will become a key concern, especially over urban areas prone to 
flooding. The NWS Weather Prediction Center (WPC) has placed the 
entire Florida peninsula under a Marginal Risk (at least 5% 
chance) of Excessive rainfall through Monday. 

High temperatures today will hit the low-mid 90s across most areas. 
Peak heat index values will be highly dependent on rain and 
thunderstorm activity, along with cloud cover. Areas experiencing 
less cloud cover could have heat index values in the 105F and 110F 
range. 

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Monday night through Saturday)
Issued at 403 AM EDT Sun Aug 30 2026

Models push a TUTT feature over the state further eastward, while a 
sfc frontal boundary moves across the SE CONUS. Meanwhile, the W Atl 
ridge axis will linger just north of the state through the rest of 
the week, keeping a generally E/SE flow in place across SoFlo. 

Moisture advection will persist during the long term and keeping 
tropical moisture in place, with model PWATs remaining above 
seasonal normals around or above 2" through the work week. This will 
continue to support scattered to numerous showers and storms each 
afternoon, with convection initiating along the East coast sea 
breeze boundary, then pushing inland during the late afternoon 
hours. Hazards will include gusty winds, heavy rainfall and frequent 
lightning.

Through mid week, models show the aforementioned trough and front 
progressing eastward, with the two flanking ridges over the CONUS 
and western Atlantic starting to merge, extending across the entire 
region. Afternoon showers and thunderstorms will remain likely each 
afternoon, with coverage maximized across the interior and southwest 
FL thanks to the continuing easterly flow. The wet pattern should 
extend through the end of the work week with abundant moisture 
remaining in place. 

Temperatures through the period will remain seasonably hot, with 
highs in the low to mid 90s each afternoon and overnight lows in the 
low 80s across the coastlines, and mid 70s over the interior.

.SHORT TERM...

Issued at 232 PM EDT Sun Aug 30 2026

A persistent weak mid to upper level trough will continue to
slowly push northward across the region through tonight into
Monday. At the surface, high pressure will remain centered off to
the northeast in the Atlantic. This will allow for a light to
moderate east to southeasterly wind flow to continue across the
region into the early portion of the week. Deep layer tropical
moisture will continue to filter into the region along the east to
southeasterly wind flow and PWATs will generally range between 2.1
and 2.3 inches heading into tonight and then into Monday. 

As this evening progresses, most of the ongoing shower and 
thunderstorm activity that has developed over the interior as well
as Southwest Florida will gradually diminish due to loss of 
diurnal heating and instability. However, additional shower and 
thunderstorm activity will remain possible over the Atlantic 
waters and east coast heading into the overnight hours. Low 
temperatures tonight will generally range from the lower 70s 
across interior portions of Southwest Florida to the lower 80s 
across the east coast metro areas. 

As Monday progresses, the latest model soundings show 500mb
temperatures warming up a bit and generally ranging between -5.5
to -6.5C heading into the afternoon hours as the mid level trough
tries to slowly drift northward during this time frame. An 
abundance of moisture will remain in place and sea breeze 
development will help spark off scattered to numerous showers and 
thunderstorms as the day progresses. Coverage of showers and 
storms will remain elevated due to an abundance of moisture over 
the region, however, the typical diurnal trend will remain in 
place with storms starting out over the east coast in the morning
and midday before shifting towards the interior and west during 
the afternoon and early evening. While chances of strong
thunderstorm development will be slightly lower, it cannot be 
entirely ruled out especially over the interior and Southwest 
Florida where instability will be maximized due to peak diurnal 
heating. The strongest storms will be capable of producing heavy 
downpours and gusty winds. With PWATs over 2 inches, high rainfall
rates with the stronger thunderstorms could lead to the potential
for localized flooding across the urban and low lying areas. High
