.KEY MESSAGES...

- Hot and humid today and tomorrow with heat index values up
  around 90.

- Above normal temperatures with highs in the 80s to continue
  for the first week of September.

- Isolated showers/storms today with the next chance coming late
  Tuesday into early Wednesday.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 219 AM CDT Sun Aug 30 2026

Today and Tonight... Today's weather will be driven by warm air
advection. First and most obvious warm and moist air is moving 
in brining us higher temperatures and dew points. This will 
bring heat index values into the 90s with the higher values 
south (southern MN/west central WI) and lower north (central 
MN/northwest WI). This warm air advection will also occur along 
a warm front and the lift from this front will provide some 
chances for storm development. The challenge for CI will be 
overcoming the cap we have in place this morning. So far this 
cap has held and no development has been noted. For anything 
that does occur this morning CI will need to occur over the 
Dakotas and survive into Minnesota. We do have strong elevated 
instability, so elevated storms could maintain themselves if 
they have a deep enough updraft. This afternoon and evening 
daytime heating should help to break this cap, but the front 
will lift north such that chances will be mainly in central and 
northern Minnesota. The main severe chance will be tied more to 
the cold front moving across the Dakotas. So severe will be tied
to storms that initiate to the west and track into Minnesota 
overnight. How linear this storms go will play a big part in
determining the risk type. More linear being more wind and more
discrete favoring hail. SPC has also noted a low tornado chance
tied to the area along the warm front.

Monday and Tuesday... The cold front will pass through Minnesota on
Monday providing some relief from the moisture. This will keep
the higher dew points and therefore the heat index values above
90 in western Wisconsin. With clearer skies temperatures won't
be much cooler, if at all, in Minnesota but the lower dew points
will be noticeable. These lower dew points should spread into
Wisconsin on Tuesday expanding the relief.

Tuesday night into Wednesday... Another shortwave trough moving
across the plains will provide our next chance for rain Tuesday
night into Wednesday. Thankfully this looks more like what we
saw on Saturday morning with a more widespread light rain rather
than the more isolated nature of what is forecast for today.
Looking at forecast soundings the greatest challenge will be 
low level dry air. This means it will take a while before rain 
starts to reach the surface. This will also be a limiting factor
in strong storms, as it will greatly limit instability. Looking
towards ensemble systems there is actually good agreement for 
this far out, which is why we are already seeing higher PoPs in
the NBM. Just more of a timing displacement right now with the 
GEFS/GEPS earlier than the ENS.

Rest of the Week... Ensembles get much more dispersive after
Wednesday, but continue to show activity. This remains the same
long term forecast we have had for much of the past week with a
more active and warm pattern. This keep highs in the 80s with a 
low confidence of which days will see rain until at least the 
mid range forecast (about 3 days out).

&&

this time of year (i.e. a mean of 58 degrees for late August). So 
aside from this surface front not providing much precip today, dew

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 409 PM CDT Mon Aug 31 2026

There's an impressive bowling ball upper low over southern 
Saskatchewan and Manitoba this afternoon, which is driving a cold 
across western WI and far southeast MN. Our position south of this 
upper low puts us in its zone of subsidence and mid-level dry air, 
which means we get yet another dry cold front, which seems par for 
the course for an August that will see MSP finish the month with 
just 0.46" of rain (we average 4.34"), which is the 4th driest 
August on record and just the 8th out of 156 years where the Twin 
Cities failed to get at least 1" of rain in the month of August. 
With that said, we can't completely rule out rain in the MPX area 
this evening, but that chance is in Eau Claire and Chippewa 
counties, to the east of Chippewa Falls and Eau Claire. East of the 
cold front, it's oppressive for the last day of August, with 
temperatures in the upper 80s, dewpoints in the mid 70s, and heat 
index values in the mid 90s. All of this heat and humidity is 
translating into instability, with a pool of 3000+ j/kg of mlCAPE 
forecast develop ahead of the front. Although isolated storm chances 
look better east of the MPX area, the HRRR has been initiating 
storms in eastern Eau Claire county around 23z from the 15z run 
through its most current run (19z), so we will have to keep an eye 
on the storm potential out around Stanley and Augusta. After that, 
the rest of the night will be quiet, with drier air moving in 
limiting the fog potential in MN (where dewpoints are in the mid 50s 
across central MN). WI will still have radiational fog potential as 
they will hold on to dewpoints in the 60s through the night.

This drier airmass moving in today will stay with us through the day 
on Tuesday, with dewpoints in the upper 40s to lower 60s making 
highs Tuesday in the 80s more tolerable. 

Tuesday night is when things start to turn more active as a 
shortwave coming out of the southwest monsoon travels across 
southern MN. Most guidance shows storms developing on the nose of 
the LLJ and riding the elevated CAPE gradient east Tuesday night. 
Looking at the HREF/REFS, the pool of high muCAPE (over 3000 j/kg) 
will remain near/north of the I-80 corridor in Iowa, with the LLJ 
nosing up into northern Iowa. This all points to the MN/IA border 
being the zone most conducive to seeing thunderstorms/heavy rain, 
with a lighter overrunning precipitation area getting about as far 
north as the Twin Cities metro, which will likely mean central MN 
into northwest WI misses out on this one. Based on where the large 
scale forcing is forecast to be, the NBM this morning looked to have 
displaced it's higher PoPs/QPF a bit too far north, so did nudge 
PoPs a bit south Tuesday night to get closer to where the forcing 
is. 

Wednesday through Labor Day begins a period of high confidence in 
summer-like warmth and humidity for the first week of meteorological 
fall, but low confidence on precipitation. Figuring out severe 
weather potential comes down to figuring out where moisture (for 
said storms), forcing (something to provide large scale ascent for 
that moist air), instability (so that the ascending moist air goes 
up in a convective updraft), and wind shear (let's organize those 
storms!) all come together. The large scale weather pattern through 
the weekend will become amplified as a trough digs into the Pac NW. 
As it digs into the Pac NW, we see the ridge over the central CONUS 
amplify, with a westerly to southwest flow developing aloft locally. 
This setup will pump deep moisture into our region from the Gulf and 
southwest Monsoon. Looking at the 4 ingredients, we'll have plenty 
of moisture (mean EPS Pwats are 150% to 200% of normal through the 
weekend), given the heat and humidity, instability will be ample, 
and with the upper jet always overhead/nearby, we'll have ample wind 
shear as well. The big uncertainty through the weekend is the 
forcing variable. With the building upper ridge, forcing looks 
subtle, with precipitation chances tied to where the warm front is 
on a daily basis and where any weak waves move through in the upper 
flow. In other words, it's mesoscale features that will be driving 
our precipitations, which is hard to parse out more than 48 hours in 
advance. The result is what you get with this forecast, numerous low 
chances for precipitation through the holiday weekend. At this 
point, about the best we can say is whatever we get, it looks to be 
predominately nocturnal in nature. Will we manage to finally cash in 
on a potential active weather pattern? Maybe, but when it comes to 
forecasting precipitation in a drought, I like to live be the maxim 
of when in drought, leave it out.

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 409 PM CDT Mon Aug 31 2026

There's an impressive bowling ball upper low over southern 
Saskatchewan and Manitoba this afternoon, which is driving a 
cold across western WI and far southeast MN. Our position south 
of this upper low puts us in its zone of subsidence and mid-
level dry air, which means we get yet another dry cold front, 
which seems par for the course for an August that will see MSP 
finish the month with just 0.46" of rain (we average 4.34"), 
which is the 4th driest August on record and just the 8th out of
156 years where the Twin Cities failed to get at least 1" of 
rain in the month of August. With that said, we can't completely
rule out rain in the MPX area this evening, but that chance is 
in Eau Claire and Chippewa counties, to the east of Chippewa 
Falls and Eau Claire. East of the cold front, it's oppressive 
for the last day of August, with temperatures in the upper 80s, 
dewpoints in the mid 70s, and heat index values in the mid 90s. 
All of this heat and humidity is translating into instability, 
with a pool of 3000+ j/kg of mlCAPE forecast develop ahead of 
the front. Although isolated storm chances look better east of 
the MPX area, the HRRR has been initiating storms in eastern Eau
Claire county around 23z from the 15z run through its most 
current run (19z), so we will have to keep an eye on the storm 
potential out around Stanley and Augusta. After that, the rest 
of the night will be quiet, with drier air moving in limiting 
the fog potential in MN (where dewpoints are in the mid 50s 
across central MN). WI will still have radiational fog potential
as they will hold on to dewpoints in the 60s through the night.

This drier airmass moving in today will stay with us through the
day on Tuesday, with dewpoints in the upper 40s to lower 60s 
making highs Tuesday in the 80s more tolerable. 

Tuesday night is when things start to turn more active as a  
shortwave coming out of the southwest monsoon travels across 
southern MN. Most guidance shows storms developing on the nose 
of the LLJ and riding the elevated CAPE gradient east Tuesday 
night. Looking at the HREF/REFS, the pool of high muCAPE (over 
3000 j/kg) will remain near/north of the I-80 corridor in Iowa, 
with the LLJ nosing up into northern Iowa. This all points to 
the MN/IA border being the zone most conducive to seeing 
thunderstorms/heavy rain, with a lighter overrunning 
precipitation area getting about as far north as the Twin Cities
metro, which will likely mean central MN into northwest WI 
misses out on this one. Based on where the large scale forcing 
is forecast to be, the NBM this morning looked to have displaced
it's higher PoPs/QPF a bit too far north, so did nudge PoPs a 
bit south Tuesday night to get closer to where the forcing is. 

Wednesday through Labor Day begins a period of high confidence
in summer-like warmth and humidity for the first week of 
meteorological fall, but low confidence on precipitation. 
Figuring out severe weather potential comes down to figuring out
where moisture (for said storms), forcing (something to provide
large scale ascent for that moist air), instability (so that 
the ascending moist air goes up in a convective updraft), and 
wind shear (let's organize those storms!) all come together. The
large scale weather pattern through the weekend will become 
amplified as a trough digs into the Pac NW. As it digs into the 
Pac NW, we see the ridge over the central CONUS amplify, with a 
westerly to southwest flow developing aloft locally. This setup 
will pump deep moisture into our region from the Gulf and 
southwest Monsoon. Looking at the 4 ingredients, we'll have 
plenty of moisture (mean EPS Pwats are 150% to 200% of normal 
through the weekend), given the heat and humidity, instability 
will be ample, and with the upper jet always overhead/nearby, 
we'll have ample wind shear as well. The big uncertainty through
the weekend is the forcing variable. With the building upper 
ridge, forcing looks subtle, with precipitation chances tied to 
where the warm front is on a daily basis and where any weak 
waves move through in the upper flow. In other words, it's 
mesoscale features that will be driving our precipitations, 
which is hard to parse out more than 48 hours in advance. The 
result is what you get with this forecast, numerous low chances 
for precipitation through the holiday weekend. At this point, 
about the best we can say is whatever we get, it looks to be 
predominately nocturnal in nature. Will we manage to finally 
cash in on a potential active weather pattern? Maybe, but when 
it comes to forecasting precipitation in a drought, I like to 
live be the maxim of when in drought, leave it out.

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Active weather will persist through Monday with periods of
  showers and thunderstorms, some potentially producing strong
  winds and heavy rainfall across south-central Arizona. 

- A Flood Watch is in effect for south-central Arizona for Sunday
  evening into Sunday night as heavy rainfall could result in 
  localized amounts in excess of 1-2 inches and flash flooding.

- Near to slightly below normal temperatures are expected for the
  first part of this week before returning to slightly above
  normal during the latter part of the week as drier conditions 
  settle over the region.

&&

.SHORT TERM /TODAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
The atmosphere will remain well primed for additional rounds of
showers and thunderstorms today and Monday with heavy rainfall a
continued concern across south-central and eastern Arizona. 
Current objective analysis shows the subtropical ridge now 
positioned across the Southern Plains, but still extending into 
southeast Arizona. A Pacific trough centered over the Pacific 
Northwest is slowly making headway through the Western U.S. with 
the southern fringes of the trough now moving into northwest 
Arizona and southern California. Moisture levels did improve a bit
on Saturday, but we are still fighting against some drier air 
aloft getting pulled in from the southwest. Very strong heating on
Saturday definitely helped to raise instability levels and much 
of that remains, except for far eastern Arizona where widespread 
rainfall occurred.

South southwesterly flow today into Monday should improve lower 
level moisture across most of Arizona, but the drier air aloft 
will continue to stream into southern California into western
Arizona. Low level mixing ratios through Monday are forecast to
be between 10-12 g/kg, just enough to worry about a heavy rainfall
threat due to the forecast MUCAPE of 1000-1750 J/kg across the 
area. Yesterday's heavy rainfall only affected higher terrain 
areas as there just wasn't enough lift to get storms to fire early
enough over the lower deserts, but that should change today. 

Guidance shows a strengthening upper level shortwave moving into
central California later today, while a secondary jet max will be
positioned to our north/northeast. The shortwave to our west is
not expected to help until at the earliest Sunday night, but the
jet max to our north will at least position central and eastern
Arizona in a favorable area of ascent. Assuming near optimal
heating conditions today, at least over south-central Arizona,
forecast MUCAPEs should rise to around 1500 J/kg by late afternoon
providing plenty of instability for storms to develop. Forecast
soundings also show very little CIN during the latter half of the
afternoon which should even allow for some scattered storms to 
initiate over the lower deserts. CAMs, especially the 06Z HRRR, 
show widespread showers and storms developing late in the 
afternoon across Pima, Pinal and Gila Counties before spreading 
north and northwestward through much of Maricopa County in the 
evening. A few storms may become strong enough to drop 50+ mph 
winds with western Pinal and southern Maricopa Counties likely 
being the best area for the strongest winds and dust to occur. 

Given the amount of instability and moisture levels reaching
above normal for late August, we are anticipating some areas will
receive heavy rainfall this evening into early tonight. Another 
Flood Watch has been issued for Maricopa, Pinal, and Gila Counties
for this evening into tonight with localized 1-2 inch amounts
quite possible focused across western Pinal through central 
Maricopa County this evening and then over northern Maricopa 
County during the early overnight hours. We also can't rule out 
the possibility of storms lasting longer Sunday night as the 
shortwave trough will be getting closer to western Arizona, but 
eventually we should exhaust most of the available instability.

Monday's forecast remains more uncertain as it seems likely
today/tonight will be very busy resulting in a somewhat work-over
atmosphere going into Monday morning. However, guidance still 
shows ample moisture on Monday with even better moisture in the 
mid levels compared to today. Cloud cover will likely be an issue 
for at least eastern Arizona limiting heating and instability, but
there should be decent heating and recovery over south-central 
Arizona. The track of the shortwave trough takes it more into 
southern Nevada into Utah during the first half of Monday putting 
northern Arizona more in the prime area better shear and stronger 
storms. Despite the shortwave brushing past to the northwest, we 
should again fall within a fairly favorable area of ascent over 
central Arizona due to the position of the jet max over western 
Utah/northwest Arizona. Monday's storm potential is expected to be
more conditional and more scattered compared to today, but it 
would not be surprising to see a few strong storms and localized 
heavy rainfall again. In fact, the forecast sounding for Monday in
Phoenix looks nearly identical to today.

Temperatures are finally starting to cool off with the exit of the
ridge and the increased rain activity. Highs today are expected to
top out at around 105 degrees in the Phoenix area to 106-110
degrees across the western deserts. Monday should be the 'coolest'
day of the week with the NBM calling for highs in the mid to upper
90s for Phoenix to right near normal for the western lower
deserts.

&&

.LONG TERM /TUESDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/... 
A much quieter period of weather is anticipated starting Tuesday
as the flow turns more out of the west southwest ushering much
drier air through the rest of the area. Forecast PWATs are
expected to drop to just below normal on Tuesday, likely staying
on the lower side through around Thursday. NBM PoPs drop off to 
mostly below 10% starting Tuesday and carrying through at least 
Wednesday. Temperatures will also be a bit slow to warm back up as
the trough will still have some influence over our region. 
Forecast highs return back into the normal range by Wednesday, 
while overnight lows will be a more comfortable upper 70s to low 
80s for the lower deserts.

High model uncertainty becomes an issue late week into next 
weekend as models are currently favoring a tropical cyclone to
move northwestward off the coast of Baja and potentially even
getting close to California early during the following week. It is
impossible to know at this point where this TC will go, but it at
least seems fairly likely it will help to direct moisture
northward into our region by next weekend. Assuming this occurs,
we may eventually return to busy monsoon weather.

&&

The main aviation concern this forecast period will be another round 
of thunderstorms, gusty outflow winds, and blowing dust starting 
potentially as early as late this afternoon and lasting through much 
of tonight. Until then, VFR conditions with a typical diurnal wind 
pattern is anticipated. Winds will start off light out of the E-SE 
this morning before gradually shifting out of the WSW this 
afternoon. Intermittent gusts into the teens to around 20 kts can be 
expected by the late afternoon period. 

Heading into this evening, an active period of weather is likely 
with TS and BLDU becoming the main hazards. Latest model guidance 
suggests TS will develop to the south of the terminals and gradually 
build into the Phoenix Metro along a northward progressing outflow. 
Some models do develop convection earlier today (possibly as early 
as 22Z-00Z) and thus timing may need to be adjusted in later 
issuances. For now, the best timing of arrival of the outflow and 
subsequent TS looks to be around 01Z at KIWA and 02Z at the 
remaining TAF sites. Strong S-SE winds >30 kts will likely accompany 
the outflow along with vsbys around 2-4 SM in BLDU. Periods of 
VCTS/TSRA can also be anticipated and will last for several hours. 
Another round of SHRA may also develop around the 06-10Z timeframe.
SCT mid/high cloud decks will be common through the period, with the 
lowest CIGs forecasted at 10kft during thunderstorm activity.

Southeast California/Southwest Arizona including KIPL and KBLH: 

No major aviation concerns are expected at the SE California 
terminals. At KIPL, winds will fluctuate between westerly and 
southeasterly with westerly winds increasing again by this evening. 
At KBLH, winds will fluctuate between southerly and southwesterly 
through the TAF period. Speeds will be elevated (10-15 kt) most of 
the period with some gusts of 20-25kt during the afternoon and early 
evening. Skies will be mostly clear with FEW-SCT mid and high clouds 
moving into the region by this evening.

east of the area over the southern Plains while a broad trough 
encompasses much of the western 1/3 of the CONUS. This pattern 
configuration is resulting the flow to be out of the south-
southwest, aiding with maintaining elevated moisture levels across 
the region as the latest SPC mesoanalysis shows PWATs of 1.5"+ 
across much of the AZ lower deserts and between 1.1-1.5" across the 
higher terrain areas along with 10-12 g/kg of low-level mixing 
ratios. The elevated moisture combined with 500 mb temperatures 
cooling to between -7C to -8C will result MLCAPE values later this 
afternoon into early this evening to peak at around 1500 J/KG. The 
favorable thermodynamic environment combined with better ascent due 
to increasing upper-level divergence from a jet streak moving 
through the Great Basin will result in favorable conditions for the 
development of widespread storm activity across much of south-
central AZ, especially from early this evening into the overnight
period.

Latest hi-res guidance, similar to yesterday, shows storms 
developing across the AZ High Country as well as southeast AZ by the 
early to mid afternoon hours. The activity across southeast AZ will 
eventually send an outflow northward that will likely spark 
additional storms into Pinal and Maricopa Counties with activity 
affecting the Phoenix area heading this evening. Latest forecast 
soundings for late this afternoon into early evening show a nearly
uncapped atmosphere once again and thus it will take just a 
single outflow to result in convective initiation across the 
lower deserts. Initially with the storms, strong downburst wind 
gusts and areas of blowing dust in the dust prone areas will be 
the primary hazards as DCAPE values will be high once again, 
peaking at 1500 J/KG before heavy rainfall and flash flooding 
eventually become the more primary hazard. Given the potential for
more heavy rainfall that could produce localized amounts of 1-2" 
and thus lead to flash flooding, a Flood Watch is in effect for 
much of south-central AZ starting early this evening and 
continuing through the overnight period. There is a potential that
storms may last into the overnight period as some of the hi-res 
guidance is showing given that an upper-level shortwave trough 
will be approaching from the northwest that may aid in sustaining 
the convective activity for a longer period of time with heavy 
rainfall/flash flooding being the primary hazard.

The forecast for Monday remains a bit uncertain as everything 
will be more conditional as to what happens later today into the 
overnight period and how fast the atmosphere can recover. If the 
atmosphere is able to recover fast enough where decent instability
develops, then another round of enhanced shower and thunderstorm 
activity will be likely once again as the upper-level shortwave 
will be positioned to the north-northwest over southern Nevada and
Utah, providing good upper-level ascent across much of central 
AZ. Latest forecast soundings show very favorable thermodynamic 
profiles once again with MLCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/KG along 
with a uncapped atmosphere, supporting the potential for some 
robust thunderstorms. However, this is assuming that the 
atmosphere is able to fully recover from the activity that is 
likely to materialize later today through the overnight period. 

With the subtropical ridge now positioned well east of the area, 
temperatures this afternoon will be noticeably cooler as readings 
top out in the low to mid 100s across the south-central AZ lower 
deserts and in the mid to upper 100s across the western deserts. 
Even cooler temperatures are forecast for Monday, especially across 
south-central AZ, where more abundant cloud cover and potential 
rainfall may limit afternoon highs to just the middle to upper 90s 
while warmer readings in the mid 100s are expected for the western 
deserts.

as the flow turns more out of the west southwest ushering much

expected to drop to just below normal on Tuesday, likely staying
on the lower side through around Thursday. NBM PoPs drop off to

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Flood Watches cover much of southern and central Arizona today 
  as periods of showers and thunderstorms, capable of producing 
  heavy rainfall, will remain possible.

- Quiet weather under mostly clear skies is expected for Tuesday
  and Wednesday before potentially another more active period of
  weather materializes by the end of the week into the weekend.

- Near to slightly below normal temperatures are expected
  throughout much of the week. 

&&

.SHORT TERM /TODAY INTO TONIGHT/...
Scattered showers and thunderstorms continue to impact portions 
of south-central and eastern Arizona early this morning, some of 
which continue to produce gusty (sub-severe) wind gusts and 
localized moderate rainfall. Much of the available instability 
that built up yesterday has been exhausted, but a narrow corridor 
of 500-1000 J/kg of elevated CAPE remains from east of Phoenix 
northwestward through northern Maricopa County into Yavapai 
County. Showers and storms should mainly be focused east of 
Phoenix through the rest of the morning with localized rainfall 
amounts of an inch or so still a possibility. The Flood Watch has 
been extended through noon for Pinal and Gila Counties and the 
eastern half of the Phoenix Metro. Given this activity is expected
this morning, it is likely to ruin any chances for organized
activity east of Phoenix during the afternoon hours. 

Looking more broadly across the region, the main driver of the
shower and thunderstorm activity stems from a shortwave trough
digging eastward through the southern half of California and a 
jet streak positioned across northern Arizona through Utah. 
Moisture levels across most of Arizona remain quite good with low 
level mixing ratios of 11-13 g/kg and PWATs around 150% of normal.
Given the continued broad forced ascent over much of the area 
persisting through at least this afternoon, additional rounds of 
showers and thunderstorms are likely. The best area of focus by 
this afternoon should switch to over western Maricopa County and 
La Paz County and possibly int northern Yuma County. This area 
will likely see a decent amount of sunshine later this morning and
this afternoon to rebuild the instability with HREF MUCAPEs again
reaching between 1000-1500 J/kg for this afternoon. CAMs 
generally agree scattered thunderstorms are likely to develop from
around Tucson through southern/western Maricopa County by mid to 
late afternoon with more isolated storms across La Paz County. 
Some of these storms may result in strong gusty winds, but the 
severe threat remains quite low. Additional rainfall amounts of up
to or just over 1" will also be possible in these areas resulting
in a renewed localized flash flood threat. Flood Watches have 
been extended across western Maricopa County through early this 
evening and also expanded into La Paz and northern Yuma Counties 
for this afternoon through early evening. 

As the shortwave trough lifts northeastward into Nevada this
afternoon and into Utah this evening, we will gradually lose our
upper level support leaving only slight chances for a few showers
during the overnight hours tonight.

&&

.LONG TERM /TUESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/... 
West southwesterly drier flow aloft will spread over the rest of
Arizona by Tuesday with a brief time period of anticyclonic flow 
aloft. The drier air aloft is expected to mix into the boundary 
layer by Tuesday afternoon dropping surface dew points into the 
40s across southeast California to 55-60 degrees in the Phoenix 
area. Although we can't rule out a few isolated showers or weak 
thunderstorms Tuesday afternoon over the more favored higher 
terrain locations, the chances are only around 10-15%. 
Temperatures will remain below normal across south-central and 
eastern Arizona with lower desert highs at around 100 degrees, 
while the drier western lower deserts should reach closer to 105 
degrees. 

The drying aloft will continue to a lesser degree into Wednesday
as low level mixing ratios drop to 5-6 g/kg in southeast
California to 7-9 g/kg across much of Arizona. Chances for any
showers and storms should be similar or even less than Tuesday's
chances. Temperatures should also warm another couple of degrees
under sunny to mostly sunny skies.

Forecast concern is increasing for the potential of tropical 
moisture surging northward into the region as early as Thursday 
night into Friday, but more so for the coming weekend. NHC shows a
tropical disturbance currently near 10N and 107W with a 90% 
chance of cyclone formation this week and likely tracking 
northward off the coast of Baja by Friday into the weekend. There 
is still a lot of uncertainty with this potential tropical 
system, but model guidance has been coming to a bit better 
consensus the last several model runs. Roughly 90% of the GEFS and
EPS members now show PWATs increasing to 1.8-2.2" over portions of 
our area by Friday or Saturday. Given this likely increase in 
moisture, PoPs have gone up starting Friday and continue through 
the weekend. It will likely be at least 2 or 3 more days until we 
have a good idea on what would likely happen late this week. 
Getting tropical moisture into our region is definitely not 
unusual, but many times when it happens we struggle to build 
instability due to extensive cloudiness and poor lapse rates. 
However, it seems quite likely a Pacific trough will be situated 
along or just off the West Coast which may provide for enough 
upper level forced ascent to overcome the likely lackluster 
instability. We will continue to watch this throughout the week as
it very well could lead to another round of heavy rainfall at 
some point.

West southwesterly drier flow aloft will spread over the rest of
Arizona by Tuesday with a brief time period of anticyclonic flow 
aloft. The drier air aloft is expected to mix into the boundary 
layer by Tuesday afternoon dropping surface dew points into the 
40s across southeast California to 55-60 degrees in the Phoenix 
area. Although we can't rule out a few isolated showers or weak 
thunderstorms Tuesday afternoon over the more favored higher

eastern Arizona with lower desert highs at around 100 degrees, 
while the drier western lower deserts should reach closer to 105

chances. Temperatures should also warm another couple of degrees
under sunny to mostly sunny skies.

moisture surging northward into the region as early as Thursday 
night into Friday, but more so for the coming weekend. NHC shows a

northward off the coast of Baja by Friday into the weekend. There 
is still a lot of uncertainty with this potential tropical 
system, but model guidance has been coming to a bit better 
consensus the last several model runs. Roughly 90% of the GEFS and
EPS members now show PWATs increasing to 1.8-2.2" over portions of 
our area by Friday or Saturday. Given this likely increase in 
moisture, PoPs have gone up starting Friday and continue through 
the weekend. It will likely be at least 2 or 3 more days until we

unusual, but many times when it happens we struggle to build 
instability due to extensive cloudiness and poor lapse rates.

along or just off the West Coast which may provide for enough 
upper level forced ascent to overcome the likely lackluster 
instability. We will continue to watch this throughout the week as

.SHORT TERM /TODAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/...
Latest water vapor satellite imagery shows a well-defined upper-
level shortwave over southern Nevada and is the main feature that
drove the widespread rainfall activity that was observed across 
much of south-central AZ throughout the morning hours. Rainfall 
intensity has been on the light to locally moderate side and thus 
rainfall accumulations for the most part have remained under 0.3",
with some localized areas observing amounts up to 0.5". Most of 
this activity has moved east of Phoenix and will be ending in Gila
County during the early afternoon hours. The overworked atmosphere
from the morning activity will essentially end the potential for
more organized convective activity for the rest of today for
much of south-central AZ. The main focus for convection for this 
afternoon will shift west of Phoenix, across portions of La Paz 
into northern Yuma County as well as western Maricopa County as 
ample heating will cause MLCAPE values to peak at 1500-2000 J/KG, 
which is more than sufficient for strong thunderstorms to develop.
Although strong downburst wind gusts will be possible, the 
primary hazard will be heavy rainfall leading to flash flooding 
with localized amounts in excess of 1-2" possible, especially with
any training cells. As the upper-level shortwave lifts 
northeastward into Utah by this evening, much of the upper-level 
support will be lifting to the north as well and thus activity 
should diminish by the early evening hours with quieter conditions
expected during the late evening and overnight hours tonight.

Quieter weather is expected Tuesday and Wednesday as significantly 
drier air due to west-southwest mid-level flow will overspread the 
region, especially in the mid to upper levels with strong subsidence 
aloft. A few isolated storms will still be possible Tuesday 
afternoon, mainly across the terrain escarpments given that 
boundary level moisture will still be sufficient with mixing 
ratios above 10 g/kg. However, by Wednesday, mixing ratios will 
have dropped to less than 10 g/kg with little to no instability 
expected and thus storm chances should be completely eliminated 
across much of the CWA. 

Due to the abundant cloud cover and rainfall this morning, afternoon 
high temperatures across much of south-central AZ will likely 
struggle to reach 90 degrees while significantly warmer highs due to 
more sunshine can be expected across the western deserts as readings 
top out in the mid to upper 100s. Temperatures Tuesday and 
Wednesday, with much more sunshine, should rebound into the low 100s 
across the south-central AZ lower deserts and top out into the mid 
100s across the western deserts, with these readings near to a few 
degrees below normal for early September.

.DISCUSSION...
As of 200 PM Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... Scattered showers today with localized areas of 
heavy rainfall possible. Lesser storm coverage on Sunday, 
then turning drier for much of the week ahead.

Early afternoon water vapor imagery reveals a weak baggy trough 
aloft with broad southwesterly flow across the region. Low and mid 
level WV channels depicts a deeper plume of moisture along and east 
of US-1 with markedly drier air to the west. PW's this morning were 
sampled at around 1.4" per 12Z KGSO sounding while nearly 2.3" at 
KMHX. At the surface a weak stationary front remains stretched 
across NC from east to west (generally along US-64). This was the 
focal area for isolated shower and storm development this morning as 
a series of weak waves rode along the front.

For the remainder of today, weak forcing for ascent will drift 
northward from SC into NC which should be enough to kick off 
additional showers along and south of the stationary front which we 
are already seeing. Given the abundance of cloud cover from this 
morning, surface based and mixed layer instability will be lacking 
(still around 1500 J/KG but a far cry from the 2000-3000 J/KG that 
had been readily available the last few days). This, combined with

.DISCUSSION...
As of 220 PM Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... Anomalously hot temperatures expected to 
persist through Thursday and perhaps into Friday.

A deep subtropical ridge of around 595 dam centered over the 
Mid-Mississippi Valley in the 12z H5 RAOBs this morning is 
forecast to strengthen as it wobbles gradually eastward and 
stretching over the Carolinas by Thurs morning. Highly anomalous
H850 temperatures (at-or-above the 99.5 percentile) initially 
directed over the Mid-Mississippi Valley today, will gradually 
warm to around 20-22C and slowly be directed over the southern 
Mid-Atlantic Wed through Fri. This pattern is highly favorable 
for an early September heat wave with minimal convective chances
due to influence from the strong subtropical ridge. 

Low-lvl thicknesses and diabatic techniques line up with 
statistical guidance and supports widespread mid/upper 90s as 
early as Tues, but especially Wed into Fri. A few locations may 
reach triple digit air temperatures, but widespread GTE 100 
degrees is not expected. Heat index values in the upper 90s to 
around 105 degrees are expected each day with areas south and 
east of Raleigh most probable to surpass 105 degrees for several
hours due to better low-lvl moisture in place. Targeted heat 
advisories appear likely. Increasing convective chances, 
an approaching cold front and northeast flow in its wake should
put an end to the heat by Sun.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Labor Day weekend through Monday gradually 
trends cooler and drier with a lingering chance of showers and 
storms.

Ensemble guidance is indicating that the hot anomalous ridge of
high pressure over the area will gradually shift westward this 
coming holiday weekend. Much of the guidance is projecting the 
ridge will shift into the Midwest to Central Plains of the US by
Saturday. 

As the ridge shifts west, troughing across the Mid-Atlantic and
NE US is favored to take over. This troughing will be 
associated with a cold front that approaches Saturday and is 
forecast to push through by Sunday. Depending on how the pattern
evolves, some models suggest cool 1026-mb high pressure could 
extend into the area by Labor Day, favoring highs for the latter
part of this weekend and into Monday in the low to middle 80s. 
Dewpoints could dip into the 50s on Monday, a welcome change.

Ahead of the front, we should see storm chances increase. Those
chances may initially start Friday with a pre-frontal trough, 
but better coverage is expected Saturday ahead of the front. 
Isolated or scattered storms could linger into Sunday, though 
drier conditions are favored as we head into Labor Day. Right 
now, we are not outlooked from SPC. However, their long-range 
discussion does indicate a possible severe risk over the 
Carolinas Saturday ahead of the front. Predictability, however, 
is too low at this time, but will be monitored as we go through 
the week.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z MONDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
As of 200 PM Monday...

Prevailing VFR conditions are expected to persist through the 
24 hour TAF period. Isolated to scattered showers and perhaps 
infrequent lightning will be possible around the VA/NC border 
this afternoon, and perhaps as far south as RDU/RWI, but better 
chances around GSO/INT. Marginal instability and weak shear 
should only result in short-lived showers with additional 
development possible along subsequent outflow boundaries. Shower
activity should quickly abate around sunset with loss of 
diurnal heating. Lingering low level moisture across the Coastal
Plain and Sandhills may result in another round of LIFR 
stratus/mist or fog early Tues morning, but confidence is low 
enough to preclude addition in the 18z TAFs; most probable at 
FAY.

Outlook: Afternoon convection will likely be suppressed Tuesday
through Thursday with mostly fair weather cu around 5-8 kft 
during the afternoon hours. Light and variable winds persist 
generally out of the southwest. Shower/storm chances increase 
Fri and especially Sat as the ridge breaks down and a cold front
approaches from the north-northeast on Sat.

Tuesday with increasing clouds. Although Tuesday is expected to
be predominantly dry into the afternoon for most locations, a
few showers begin to increase in the afternoon, with a 10%
probability of thunderstorms in the Cascades late due to
increasing south flow aloft.

out of the NE Pacific into the offshore waters on Wednesday.
This system will bring widespread rain into Western Washington
Wednesday through Thursday. The heaviest rainfall is expected
over the Olympic Peninsula given the vicinity of the upper low,
however, measurable rainfall is expected for all locations. In 
addition to the rain, gusty winds are expected, especially for 
early September standards, as noted on the ECMWF EFI. NBM 
highlights the probability for wind gusts exceeding 40 MPH 
between 30 to 70% for the immediate coast, Whidbey Island, San 
Juan Islands, and western Whatcom County. Elsewhere, gusts of 25
to 35 MPH are forecast at this time. Given the vegetation on 
trees, early season wind impacts such as blown down tree limbs 
and isolated power outages can't be ruled out. Temperatures drop
into the 60s on Wednesday due to the presence of the stronger 
system by midweek.

lightning threat in heavier showers. Although winds will be
lighter on Thursday, continued south winds remain locally
breezy. Ensembles are in good agreement of troughing over Oregon
and Washington Friday into Saturday. The rain threat is expected
to slowly diminish during this period, but wrap around moisture
may still bring continued precipitation to some areas.

ensembles do begin to show troughing slowly moving eastwards
heading into next week. JD

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 1224 AM CDT Mon Aug 31 2026

Another hot day is in the books with no new records, but continued
triple digits over east Texas will linger another day or two. We
did have one lonely shower today near Sam Rayburn south of
Pineland in the mid afternoon. And while most of us will see 
little change to our pattern in the short term, we could see a few
showers and isolated thunderstorms edge toward our southern tier 
of counties and parishes late on Monday or early evening. 

Of course, this is in response to the building disturbance in the
northern Gulf. The National Hurricane Center will see data from 
an Air Force reconnaissance flight early on Monday and have a much
better handle on conditions. For now, the water vapor and 
lightning detection both show the area of convection is expanding 
with several hot spots that could wrap up a core very quickly over
the warm Gulf. The disturbance is 125 miles S of Grand Isle and 
is drifting west northwestward. A depression or Tropical storm 
may soon form and would be named Edouard. 

The short term models are in good agreement with an upper core 
low weakness at 588dam, with the GFS taking the lead on the 
surface reflection wrapping up to 1006mb. The ECMWF is likewise, 
but not as deep 1010mb. Both sport a low level circulation in the
latest run. So far, the system is fairly compact with impacts for
our area not expected on Monday aside from some approaching 
convection late day. However, if well organized, some of this 
activity could end moving into our area by sunset and into the 
evening hours.
 
Our forecast for Tuesday and Wednesday are already building the 
solid rain chances into our area already, and if the storm wraps 
up, these high chances will become more widespread likely. The WPC
is high lighting Marginal EROs for our deep east Texas counties. 
So make sure and keep tabs on this potential for needed rainfall. 
Aside from all eyes on the Gulf, the remnants of Dolly are moving 
into the Leeward Islands and Bahamas and could end up helping out 
too, as a good cold front drops across the Great Lakes and Ohio 
Valley. This will dampen the migrating upper ridge and weaken it 
completely by midweek. This opens the door for the upper heat ridge
to reform over the plains and intermountain west by late week. 
The GFS builds it to 597 dam, but the ECMWF likes more with 599dam
by Labor Day and both over Nebraska. So our weekend may not be so
hot with more clouds and decent rain chances arriving as the Ohio
Valley surface high is reinforced, which will help to backdoor 
the boundary into the lower and middle MS River Valley. 

Coverage will be mainly along and east of I-49, but very subject 
to change. A Pacific cyclone could soon form from a couple of 
strong disturbances out there south and southeast of Baja. One is 
70% like the New Orleans disturbance and the other is more likely 
at 90% chance of formation. This is what the models both quickly 
wrap up late next weekend. So suffice it to say, the month of 
September generally sees the peak of tropical activity and will 
bear watching for much of the country. /24/
